Physiology of hemostasis

Hemostatic System

•Definition:It is a process which causes bleeding to stop, meaning to keep blood within a damaged blood vessel.

•The Hemostatic system is therefore composed of two antagonizing forces which must be in balance with each-others: I-Procoagulant forces: Forces which act to keep blood inside the blood vessels which are: 1-Components of the primary hemostasis: a-Blood vessels walls. b-Platelets. 2-Components of the secondary hemostasis:The coagulation factors. II-Anticoagulant forces: Forces which act to keep blood in a fluid state which are: 1-Natural anticoagulants. 2-Fibrinolytic system. 4

Original page 5

Procoagulant forces

Blood vessels

Role of the vascular endothelium in hemostasis:

I-Mechanical role:

–Smooth: prevents platelet adhesion and contact activation of coagulation factors

–Intact: prevents bleeding or blood exposure to the subendothelial collagen.

–Positively charged: Repell platelets.

–Small gaps: covered with platelets.

II-Chemical and biological roles:

1-Substances causing vasodilatation and inhibitors of platelet aggregation:

A-Prostacyclin (PGI2):

–Origin: Endothelial cells, fibroblasts and smooth muscles.

–Inducers: Thrombin, high blood pressure and trauma.

–Platelets receptors: prostacyclin receptors.”G-protein coupled receptors”.

–Action: Stimulation of adenylate cylase → conversion of ATP into cAMP → ↑ cAMP → ↓ calcium release → VD and ↓ platelet aggregation.

–Half-life: Few minutes and degraded into inactive 6 keto prostaglandin F.

B-Nitric oxide (Endothelial cell relaxing factor):

–Origin: a-Continuous secretion: from smooth muscles, macrophages, activated platelets and endothelial cells. b-Inducible secretion: from endothelial cells stimulated by inflammatory cytokines as IL1, tumor necrosis factor and endotoxins.

–Action: stimulation of guanyle cyclase → ↑ c GMP → stimulation of protein kinases → ↑ c AMP → ↓ release of calcium → VD and ↓ platelets aggregation.

–Half-life: 3-5 seconds → oxidation into inactive nitrite or nitrate. C-Ecto-ADPase (CD39):It degrades ATP and ADP → inhibition of platelet aggregation in response to thrombin. 5

○Thrombospondin-1

–Inducers: activation of platelets by thrombin.

–Receptors on platelets: Integrins (αIIb β3, αV β3 and CD36), integrin associated proteins and integrin bound fibrinogen and fibronectin

–Action: Binding to integrin associated proteins → Activation of the αIIb β3 glycoprotein → platelet spreading and aggregation.

○Endothelin:

–Action: a-VC and ↑ platelet aggregation. b-Stimulation of growth factors and cytokines secretion. c-Stimulation of neutrophil adhesion. d-Chemotaxis for macrophages.

Selectin and P-Selectin.: Leukocyte and platelet adhesion, inflammation, phagocytosis and vascular permeability.

Platelets

•Megakaryopoiesis: The process of platelet production.

•Hematopoietic stem cells → common myeloid progenitors → megakaryocyte- erythroid progenitor → megakaryocytes → growth by endomitosis → Inward invagination encircles a part of the cytoplasm of the megakaryocyte with pseudopodia formation (Pro-platelets) → pass through blood sinusoids → release of platelets into the circulation. Each megakaryocyte give about 2000-3000 which remain 2 days in the spleen and then are released into the circulation.

Platelets distribution

–(1/3) of body platelets is in the spleen.

–(1/3) of body platelets is in the circulation.

–(1/3) of body platelets covers the gaps between the endothelial cells in the blood vessels wall.

•Normal range in adults: 150-450 X 10/L. 9

•Life span: 10 days.

Transcriptional factors required for megakaryopoiesis

1-RUNX1. 2-GATA1. 3-FOG1. 7

Inhibitory factors

a-Platelet products: Transforming growth factorβ and platelet factor 4. b-Non-platelet products: Interferone γ, Interferone α, IL1, IL4 and lekemia inhibitory factor.

Morphology

Platelets are disc shaped.

–Size: 0.5 X 3  with mean platelet volume about 7-11 fl.

Structure

1-Peripheral zone formed of: a-External coat containing the surface receptors. b-Tri-laminar membrane formed of lipid bilayer consisting of phospholipids and chlolesterol and proteins. c-Submembranous area which consists of:

➢Microtubules formed of tubulin protein: Responsible for the disc shape of the resting platelets and contraction of activated platelets.

➢Microfilaments consisting of actin and myocin: Responsible for the pseudopodia formation and platelet release reactions.

➢Canaliculi: Increase the surface area and release the content of the granules. 2-Sol gel zone: Gel like substance to support organelles containing: A-Organelles as mitochondria and Golgi apparatus. B-Granules: a-Alpha granules: about 80 copies in each platelet which contain:

➢Platelet factor 4 (PF4) and β thromboglobulin (βTG): Neutralize the anticoagulant activity of heparin-like substances present on the surface of endothelial cells.

➢Platelet derived growth factor (PDGF): Wound healing.

➢Fibronectin.

➢Von-Willebrand factor (VWF).

➢Thrombospondin. 9

Original page 10

➢Coagulation factors: Fibrinogen, Factor V and Factor VIII.

➢Plasminogen activator inhibitor (PAI).

➢High molecular weight kininogen (HMWK).

➢Protein S (PS).

➢Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI).

➢P-selectin, integrins and CD40 ligand. b-Dense granules: about 5-9 copies in each platelet which contain: Calcium, ADP, ATP and serotonin. c-Glycogen granules. d-Lysozyme granules. C-No nucleus, but residual mRNA can synthesize some functional proteins. N.B.: Factor XI: bound to PLT membrane and Factor XIII: PLT cytoplasm.

Platelets receptors

I-G-protein coupled receptors (seven-transmembrane receptors): G proteins are specialized proteins with the ability to bind GTP and GDP: 1-ADP receptors: Important for Calcium mobilization, shape changes, release reaction, production of thromboxane A2, αIIbβ3 activation and aggregation: a.P2Y:1Initiation of shape change and formation of pseudopodia. b.P2Y12: Amplificationand stabilization. 2-Thrombin receptors: PAR1 and PAR4:

–A decrease in intracellular cAMP concentration with activation of calcium release.

–Release of ADP and other contents from platelet dense granules.

–Exposure of P‐selectin from alphagranules.

–Release of granule contents enhances the activation of platelet integrins and supports the growth and stability of the platelet plug. 10

Original page 11

3-Thromboxane A2 (TP) receptors:They activate phospholipase A2 and phospholipase C and amplify platelet activation by autocrine mechanism. 4-Prostacyclin (IP) receptors:They are the major inhibitory prostaglandin which keep the platelets in the resting state. 5-Epinehrine (α2a adrenergic) receptors:Epinephrine is a weak platelet agonist → ↓ Adnylate cyclase → ↓ cAMP → ↑ calcium response of other agonists but does not induce a detectable calcium response in the absence of additional agonist. 6-Platelet activating factor (PAF) receptors:They mediate inflammation, anaphylaxis, platelet aggregation and degranulation. 7-5-hydroxytryptamin 2A (5-HT2A): Initiation ofcalcium signaling → ↑ Release reaction and platelet aggregation induced by other agonists but serotonin itself cannot cause platelet aggregation 8-Other G-protein coupled receptors: Receptors stem cell derived factor‐1 and vasopressin.

II-Integrins:

1-GPαIIbβ3 (GPIIb IIIa): It is a receptor for Fibrinogen, Von-Weillbrand factor, Fibronectin ADP, thrombin, collagen, thromboxane A2, epinephrine and Vitronectin → Aggregation, Clot retraction, Fibrinogen capture and ++ concentration in α granules, Activation of the Na/H exchanger, Intracellular calcium increase and Tyrosine phosphorylation of several proteins with Interaction of signaling molecules with the cytoskeleton. 11

Original page 12

2-GPα1β2: It is a receptor for Laminin → Adhesion. 3-GPα2β1 (GPIa/IIa): It is a receptor for Collagen→ Adhesion. 4-GPα3β1: Ligand forfibrinogen and Von-Weillbrand factor. 5-GPα3β2:Ligand forfibrinectin → Adhesion. 6-GPα5β1: Ligand forvitronectin → Adhesion. 7-GPα5β3: Ligand forvitronectin, Fibrinogen, Von-Willebrand factor, Prothrombin, Thrombospondin and Osteopontin in atherosclerotic plaques → Adhesion and Platelet-leukocyte interaction. 8-GPα6β1: Ligand for Laminin → Adhesion and shape change. 9-GPαLβ1 (CD102)/ Intercellular adhesion molecule 2 (ICAM-2): Platelet- leukocyte interaction. III-Selectins: Adhesion.

1.P-selectin (CD62p)/ Granule membrane protein (GMP)140/ Platelet

activation-dependent granule-external membrane (PADGEM):

Attachment toneutrophils and monocytes to the platelets and endothelial cells and recruitment of monocyte-derived microparticles. 2.C-type lectin-like receptor-2 (CLEC-2): receptor for podoplanin and rhodocytin → platelet aggregation. 3.CD72. 12

IV-Tyrosine kinase receptors:They act as receptors for cytokines, growth factors, hormones and other signaling molecules.

V-Immunoglobulin superfamily receptors.

VI-Leucine-rich repeat (LRR) receptors.

1.GPIb-IX-V complex: Ligands for Von-Weillbrand factor and Thrombin →

–Tethering.

–Weak activation signals.

–Interaction with the cytoskeleton which is responsible for platelet deformability.

–Ristocetin induced platelet agglutination in-vitro. 2.Toll like receptors (TLRs): Platelet-neutrophil interaction and activation of the neutrophils. 3.Matrix metalloproteinases (MMP): Adhesion, Enhancement of aggregation and Augmentation of collagen-induced platelet activation mediated by GPVI and α2β1. VII-Tetraspanins(Tetraspans) (Transmembrane 4 superfamily): signal transducers across the cell membrane. VIII-Lysophosphatidic acid receptors (LPL-R): autocrine agonists to mediate shape changes, release reactions and platelet aggregation. 13

Function of platelets:

I-Mechanical function: Cover the endothelial gaps in blood vessels. II-Role in primary hemostasis: 1-Adhesion:

–Tethering: Von-Weillbrand factor acts as a bridge between GPIb-IX-V complex and collagen.

–Formation of membrane tethers: Extension of thin processes of the lipid bilayer by the hemodynamic force away from plateletss as far as 30 or as ten times the size of platelets.

–Activation of GPVI with low affinity to collagen.

–Activation of GPIIb/IIIa which bind to Von-Weillbrand factor and fibrinogen and GPIa/IIa which bind to collagen leading to further activation of GPVI. 14

Original page 15

2-Spreading: GPIIb/IIIa sends outside-in signals to actin leading to rounding and formation of finger-like projections called filopods. Lamellopodia fill the area between adjacent filopodia which are strengthened by the actin-myocin stress fibers with squeezing of organells and granules in the center leading to the fried egg appearance of platelets.

3-Granule secretion and thromboxane A2 formation (Primary release reaction):

❖Dense granules secret ADP.

❖Membrane phospholipid form the thromboxane A2.

❖Fusion of α granules with the membrane leading to:

–Increased expression of GPIIb/IIIa to 120000 copies per one platelet.

–Expression of P-selectin on the surface of platelets which binds to P-selectin ligand on the circulating tissue factor rich microparticles (aiding in coagulation) and white blood cells (aiding in inflammation). 4-Aggregation:fibrinogen acts as a bridge between 2 GPIIb/IIIa of 2 platelets:

–Reversible aggregation when ADP recruits other platelets leading to a loose and reversible primary plug.

–Irreversible aggregation when the extrinsic thrombin causes rupture of platelet membrane and loss of platelet morphology leading to formation of the secondary irreversible plug.

–Secondary release: Rupture of platelet membrane leads to release of the insoluble intra-platelet components and platelet phospholipids. 15

Original page 16

5-Clot retraction: GPIIb/IIIa signals link the cytoplasmic actin to the surface bound fibrinogen and sends intracellular signals to myocin leading to contraction of the cytoskeleton and squeezing fluids out of the clot.

III-Procoagulant functions of platelets:

1-Phospholipids: They provide a negatively charged surface for assembly of tenase and prothrombinase complexes. Gamma carboxylation of the terminal glutamic acid of vitamin K dependent factors allows their calcium dependent binding to phospholipids. Platelet phospholipid surfaces are:

–Release of microparticles from activated platelets.

–Externalization of phosphatidyle-serine to the membrane outer leaflet. 2-Activation of factor XI in the presence of:

–Traces of ADP: Contact product coagulant activity.

–Collagen: Collagen induced coagulant activity. 3-Activation of factor XII:in the presence of ADP and Kallekrin (Fluid phase activation).

4-Coagulation factors: Platelets contain coagulation factors either in:

–Platelet granules as platelet factor 4, fibrinogen, factor V and factor VIII.

–Platelet cytoplasm: Factor XIII.

–Platelet membrane: Factor XI.

5-Role of platelets in fibrinolysis:

–Activated platelets bind plasminogen and plasminogen activators via the GPIIb/IIIa complex activating fibrinolysis by localizing plasminogen and promoting its activation. 16

Original page 17

–Thrombospondin released from platelet granules and then expressed on the platelet surface binds plasminogen and enhances its activation.

–Plasmin at low concentrations enhances platelet activation and at high concentrations depresses platelet activation.

–Platelets contain and secret two fibrinolytic inhibitors, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 and α 2-antiplasmin. 6-Clot retraction: GPIIb/IIIa signals link the cytoplasmic actin to the surface bound fibrinogen and sends intracellular signals to myosin leading to contraction of the cytoskeleton and squeezing fluids out of the clot. 17

Von Willebrand factor (VWF)

•Definition: It is a glycoprotein involved in hemostasis through its roles in both platelet adhesion to the exposed collagen and carriage and stabilization of Factor VIII.

•Gene: Located onchromosome (12).

•Structure:

–It is a multimeric glycoprotein built from identical subunits. Multimers range from 500 to over 10 000 kDa and classified into low, intermediate and high molecular weight multimers.

–It has binding sites to FVIII (D3 domain), GPIb (A1 domain), collagen (A3 domain), ADAMTS13 (A2 domain), and GPIIb/IIIa (C1 domain).

–VWF-Factor VIII complex: 1.Factor VIII C which is the functional part. 2.VWF. 3.Factor VIII A which is the antigenic part.

•Origin: 1-Endothelial cells from which it can be secreted in two pathways:

–Constitutive pathway where it is secreted directly into the plasma.

–Regulated pathway where it is synthesized and stored in the Weibel Palade bodies and secreted under the effect of Stress, exercise, venous occlusion, some hormones, pregnancy, thrombin, adrenalin. histamine, vasopressin and cytokines. 2-Megakaryocytes and platelets: stored in the alpha granules and not secreted.

•Function: 1-Platelet adhesion under high shear through binding to GPIb and collagen. 2-Carriage, stabilization and protection of Factor VIII in the plasma.

•Degradation: It is degraded by the plasma metalloproteinase ADAMTS-13 (adisintegrin and metalloproteinase with a thrombospondin type 1 motif, member 13). 18

Coagulation factors

•Coagulation Factors: They are proteins essential for normal blood clotting. They are designated by Roman numerals in the order of their discovery, not their place in the coagulation sequence.

•Classification:

1-Fibrinogen group: Fibrinogen, Factor V, Factor VIII and Factor XIII:

–Found in plasma only.

–Not adsorbed by aluminum hydroxide Al(OH)3.

–Labile factors.

–Activated by thrombin. 2-Prothrombin group (vitamin K dependent): Factor II, Factor VII, Factor IX and Factor X:

–Found in plasma and serum.

–Adsorbed by aluminum hydroxide Al(OH)3.

–Stable factors.

–Vitamin K dependent for gamma carboxylation of the terminal glutamic acid which becomes the site of the calcium dependent phospholipid binding. 3-Contact group: Factor XI, Factor XII, Prekallikrein, and High molecular weight kininogen: Activated in vitro by a rough surfaces such as glass and is activated in vivo by collagen. 19

Original page 20

Factor I (Fibrinogen):

•Gene: chromosome (4).

•Site of synthesis: Mainly in the liver but small amounts are formed in the endothelial cells.

•Structure: It is a 340-kDa homodimeric glycoprotein formed oftwo trimers of polypeptide chains (Aα, Bβ and γ) with disulphide links between them. All chains are assembled with their N termini in the central E domain and extend outward in a coiled-coil arrangement. The Bβ and γ chains terminate in globular regions collectively form the D domains. The N-terminal peptide of the α and β chains are called the fibrinopeptide A and B respectively.

•Normal range: 200-400mg/dl.

•Half-life: 4 days.

•Activation: Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to release the fibrinopeptide A and B exposing binding sites of (E) domain that match complementary sites in (D) domain leading to the formation of the fibrin monomer which then undergoes polymerization by hydrogen bonds to form a friable clot that is then stabilized by the action of Factor XIII which forms lysine-glutamate covalent bonds that are then linked to the actin filaments of platelets through GPIIa/IIIa leading to clot retraction.

•Action:

–Coagulation: Platelet aggregation, clot retraction and coagulation cascade.

–Plasma osmolarity.

–Blood viscosity.

–Tissue receptor.

–Acute phase protein.

–Tissue repair.

–Fibrinolysis: Thrombin sequestration and acceleration of plasmin activation. 20

Original page 21

Factor V (Proaccelerien/Labile factor):

•Gene: chromosome (1).

•Site of synthesis: Liver.

•Structure: It has a molecular weight of 30 kDa and consists of six domains (A1-A2- B-A3-C1-C2).

•Activation: Thrombin or Factor Xa which release the B domain and cleaves Factor V into a heavy chain consisting of A1 and A2 domains and a light chain consisting of A3, C1 and C2 domains which are non-covalently bound to each-others by the calcium. N.B.: In the start of coagulation Factor V can act without activation.

•Action: Co-factor in prothrombinase complex which activates prothrobin into thrombin.

•Half-life: 12-36 hours.

•Inactivation: Activated protein C through cleavage at the arginine amino acids at the positions of 306, 506 and 679.

Factor VIII (Anti-hemophilic factor):

•Gene: chromosome (X).

•Site of synthesis: Liver and endothelial cells.

•Structure: It’s a glycoprotein with a molecular weight is 35 kDa. It has six domains (A1-A2-B-A3-C1-C2). It is released into circulation and carried on the Von Willebrand factor. Factor VIII- Von Willebrand factor complex consists of Factor VIII C (the active coagulant fraction), Factor VIII C antigen and Von Willebrand factor.

•Activation: Thrombin dissociates Factor VIII from the Von Willebrand factor then release the B domain and cleaves Factor VIII into a heavy chain consisting of A1 and A2 domains and a light chain consisting of A3, C1 and C2 domains.

•Action: Cofactor in the intrinsic tenase complex which activates Factor X.

•Half-life: 12 hours.

•Inactivation: Activated protein C cleaves it at the amino acids 336 and 562. 21

Original page 22

Factor XIII (Fibrin stabilizing factor/ Laki-Lorand factor):

•Sites: Plasma, platelets, monocytes, macrophages and precursors of these cells.

Structure

–Plasma form: It is a glycoprotein with a molecular weight of 320 kDa consisting of a hetero-tetramer of two catalytic α subunits and two carrier β subunits.

–Cellular form: It is carried inside the platelets and formed of two α subunits.

Activation: By thrombin in the presence of calcium as a cofactor

–Removal of a small peptide of α chain with the release of the activation peptide.

–Dissociation of α and β chains in the presence of calcium leading to conformational changes and exposure of the active catalytic site.

•Action: Stabilization of fibrin polymers through formation of lysine-glutamate covalent bond and Tissue repair through cross linking fibrin to fibronectin.

•Half-life: 5-9 days.

Factor II (Prothrombin):

•Gene: Located on chromosome (11).

•Site of synthesis: Liver.

•Structure: It has a molecular weight of 72 kDa and is dependent on vitamin K forγ carboxylation of the terminal glutamic acid residue by the action of vitamin K dependent carboxylase to provide the site for calcium dependent phospholipid binding.

•Activation: by prothrombinase complex (Factor Xa, Factor Va, phospholipids and calcium) which cleaves the prothrombin fragment 1.2

•Half-life: 3 days.

Action

–Procoagulant functions: Activation of Fibrinogen, Factor XI, Factor V, Cleavage of Factor VIII from Von wielbrand and activation of Factor VIII, Factor XIII, Platelet through GPV, GPIb and protease activated receptor (PAR). 22

Original page 23

–Anticoagulan function: Thrombin thrombomodulin complex activates protein C. However, it cleaves the active binding site of Protein S (the co-factor of protein C).

–Fibrinolysis: Activation of TAFI (Thrombin activated fibrinolysis inhibitor).

–Inflammation: Platelet activation, Stimulant for cytokines leading to chemotaxis of monocytes and Up-regulation of leukocyte adhesion molecules.

Factor VII (Proconvertin/Stable factor):

•Gene: Located on chromosome (13).

•Structure: It has a chemical and physical similarity to Factor X with amolecular weight of 50 kDa and is dependent on vitamin K for γ carboxylation of the terminal glutamic acid residue by the action of vitamin K dependent carboxylase to provide the site for the calcium dependent phospholipid binding.

•Activation: Tissue factor.

Action of Tissue factor-Factor VIIa complex

–More activation of Factor VII.

–Activation of Factor X.

–Activation of Factor IX.

–Activation of Factor XI.

•Half-life: 5 hours.

•Inhibition: Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI). N.B: Tissue factor (Platelet TF / CD142) previously named: Factor III or Thromboplastin:

•Sites: Expressed on the surface of cells that normally is not exposed to the blood flow, in peri-vascularadventitial cells, Skin, organ surfaces, neuroglia, vascular smooth muscle and mesenchymal surfaces. It is expressed on the endothelial cells and monocytes only when exposed to inflammatory cytokines.

•Structure: Glycoprotein and phospholipid. It has cell surface and soluble form.

•Action: Activation of Factor VII and formation of Tissue factor-Factor VIIa complex. 23

Factor IX (Christmas factor): Vitamin K dependent:

•Gene: Located on chromosome (X).

•Activation: Tissue factor-Factor VIIa complex or Factor XIa.

•Action: Share in the intrinsic tenase complex (Factor IXa, Factor VIIIa as a cofactor, phospholipid and calcium) which activates Factor X.

•Half-life: 1 day.

•Inhibition: Anti-thrombin.

Factor X (Stuart powe): Vitamin K dependent:

•Gene: Located on the long arm of chromosome (13).

•Site of synthesis: Liver.

•Structure: Closely resemble Factor VII.

Activation

–Extrinsic tenase complex: Tissue factor-Factor VIIa complex, phospholipids and Ca.

–Intrinsic tenase complex: Factor IXa, Factor VIIIa as a cofactor, phospholipids and Ca.

Action

–Part of the prothrombinase complex (Factor Xa, Factor V, phospholipid and calcium) which activates the prothrombin in to thrombin.

–It can activate Factor V.

•Half-life: 2 days.

•Inactivation: Protein Z dependent inhibitor depending on protein Z.

24

Factor XI (Plasma thromboplastin anticident):

•Gene: Located on chromosome (4).

•Site of synthesis: Liver.

•Structure molecular weight: Platelet type (220 kDa and Plasma type (160 kDa).

•Activation: Thrombin, Factor XIIa and Factor XIa itself.

•Action: Activation of Factor IX.

•Half-life: 52 hours.

•Inactivation: Protein Z dependent inhibitor but independent on protein Z.

Factor XII (Hageman factor):

•Gene: Located on the long arm of chromosome (5).

•Structure: Molecular weight: 80 kDa. Factor XIIf is formed by the action of plasmin on Factor XIIa and has a similar action as Factor XIIa.

•Activation: Contact with rough surfaces where it is cleaved into:

–Fragment with molecular weight 52 kDa: which binds to surfaces.

–Fragment with molecular weight 28 kDa: which is the active enzyme.

Action

–Conversion of prekallikrin into kallikrin which causes more activation of Factor XII.

–Binding to Factor XI forming the contact activating product which activates Factor XI.

–Increase the activation of Factor V and Factor VIII in the presence of traces of thrombin.

–Activation of fibrinolysis.

Kalikrin (Fletcher factor):

•Gene: Located on the long arm of chromosome (4).

•Forms: Plasma form which converts HMWK to bradykinin and Salivary form which converts the low molecular weight kininogen to lysyl bradykinin.

•Activation: Factor XIIa.

•Action: Activation of HMWK and fibrinolysis 25

Original page 26

High molecular weight kininogen (HMWK) (Fitzgerald factor):

•Gene: Located on the long arm of chromosome (3).

•Molecular weight: 120 kDa.

•Activation: Kalikrin which converts HMWK to bradykinin (MW: 15 k Da).

Action of HMWK (Non-enzymatic activator of the contact system)

–Increases of the activation of Factor XI by Factor XIIa.

–Increase of the activation of Factor XII by kalikrin.

–Activation of prekalikrin to kalikrin.

–It is the precursor of the bradykinin which has the following actions:

○Vasodilatation and hypotension.

○Increase of the vascular permeability.

○Smooth muscle contraction.

○Interaction with sensory nerves causing pain.

○Increase of the plasma level of uric acid in gout.

Function of the contact system:

–Increases of activation of Factor XII (Not essential).

–Activation of plasminogen through contact surface plasminogen activator (Not essential).

–Chemotaxis leading to phagocytosis and bactericidal activity (May be important).

–Activation of the complement (May be important).

–Activation of HMWK to kinin which decreases the heart rate and slows blood flow (May be important).

–Increase of the permeability of blood vessels leading to hemoconcentration and slowing of blood flow with facilitation of coagulation.

–Activation of renin angiotensin system which controls blood pressure (Not essential). 26

Physiological Anticoagulants

•Definition: They are natural chemical substances that prevent or reduce coagulation of blood.

Types of natural anticoagulants

I-Specific anticoagulants:

1-Serine protease inhibitors (SERPINs):

–Anti-thrombin (AT): the most important.

–Heparine co-factor II (HCII).

–Protein Z (PZ) andZ protein dependent inhiptor (ZPI).

–Alpha1 antitrypsin.

–Protease nexin 2.

–C1- esterase inhibitor.

–Alpha2 antiplasmin.

–Alpha2 macroglobulin.

2-Inhibitors of cofactors:

–Protein C (PC).

–Protein S (PS).

3-Tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI).

II-Non-specific anticoagulants:

–Liver uptake of the activated factors.

–Pulmonary bed filtration.

–Self-dumping due to consumption.

Laboratory assessment of coagulation factors:

1.Prothrombin time 2.Coagulation time 3.Partial thromboplastin time 4.Activated partial thromboplastin time 5.Activated clotting time 6.Fibrinogen assays 7.Thrombin time 8.Reptilase (Ancrod) time 9.Mixing experiments 10.Measurement of the level of coagulation factors 11.Parallel line bioassay of coagulation factors 12.One stage assay.

Prothrombin time (PT):

•Indication: Evaluation of the extrinsic pathway including prothrombin, Factor V, Factor VII, Factor X and fibrinogen.

•Method: Patient citrated plasma is added to thromboplastin and calcium followed by the measurement of the clotting time. The test must be performed in duplicate and the mean of results is considered the prothrombin time.

Results

1-Prothrombin time which is expressed in seconds. 2-Prothrombin concentration: Calculated from standard curves. mean of the patient plasm 3-Prothrombin ratio: mean of the control plasma Patient Prothrombin time ISI 4-International normalization ratio: ( ) Geometric mean of normal prothrombin times N.B.: International sensitivity index (ISI): The slope of the calibration curve of the used thromboplastin to the reference thromboplastin. 64

Original page 65

Normal values: t is reagent dependent

–For the rabbit thromboplastin: 11-16 seconds.

–For the recombinant thromboplastin: 10-12 seconds.

–Two seconds prolongation than the control or more is significant.

•Prolonged prothrombin time: 1-Oral anticoagulants. 2-Vitamin K deficiency. 3-Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn. 4-Malabsorption syndrome. 5-Liver diseases especially obstructive jaundice. 6-Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. 7-Deficiency of Factor VII, X, V, prothrombin or marked fibrinogen deficiency. 8-Some reagents are insensitive to Lupus anticoagulants because the high phospholipid in the reagent neutralizes the anti-phospholipid antibodies.

Coagulation time (insensitive - intrinsic):

•Indication: Evaluation of the intrinsic and common pathways.

–Method: Clean non traumatizing venipuncture → 2 ml of blood are discarded → New sample is withdrawn with a new syringe and is divided into 3 glass tubes and 0 incubated at 37 C with minimal shaking → Monitoring of clotting in the first tube every minute → monitoring of clotting in the second tube → monitoring of clotting in the third tube “clotting time”.

•Reference range: 6-11 minutes.

Causes of prolongation

1-Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. 2-Severe liver disease. 3-Massive transfusion of stored blood. 4-Heparin. 5-Severe deficiency of any coagulation factors other than Factor VII. 65

Original page 66

Partial thromboplastin time:

•Indication: Evaluates the intrinsic and common pathways.

•Method: Patient platelet poor plasma is added to phospholipids and calcium chloride followed by the measurement of the clotting time.

•Normal range: 40-60 seconds.

Causes of prolongation: as coagulation time but more sensitive.

Activated partial thromboplastin time:

•Method: Patient platelet poor plasma is added to kaolin and phospholipids for contact activation, then calcium chloride are added followed by measurement of the clotting time.

•Normal range: 26-40 seconds. Prolongation of 3 seconds more than the control or more is significant.

Causes of prolongation: as coagulation time but more sensitive.

1-Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. 2-Severe liver disease. 3-Massive transfusion of stored blood. 4-Heparin. 5-Deficiency of any coagulation factors; Factor VIII, Factor IX, Factor X, Factor V, prothrombin or fibrinogen.

Activated clotting time:

•Indication: Monitoring of very high doses of unfractionated heparin during cardiopulmonary bypass and other surgeries.

•Method: Patient whole blood is added to a surface activator as celite, glass beads or kaolin followed by measurement of the coagulation time.

•Normal range: 70 – 180 seconds. 66

Original page 67

Causes of prolongation

1-Heparin therapy. 2-Oral anticoagulants. 3-Thrombocytopenia or PLTs functional disorders. 4-Deficiency of Factor VIII, Factor IX, Factor X, Factor XI, Factor XII or fibrinogen. 5-Lupus anticoagulants. 6-Hypothermia. 7-Hemodilution. 8-Aprotinin: if celite is used.

Fibrinogen assays:

A-Clauss technique: Patient platelet poor plasma is added to a strong thrombin solution followed by measurement of the clotting time and blotting it against a standard curve prepared using different dilutions of normal plasma

•Normal range: 1.8-3.6 g/l.

•Causes of decrease: Hypofibrinogenaemia, inherited dysfibrinogenaemia and fibrin degradation products with concentrations more than 190 ug/ml. B-Prothrombin time-based: Prothrombin time is measured in reference plasma with different fibrinogen concentrations and a standard curve is drawn followed by plotting of the patient’s prothrombin time against the curve. C-Fibrinogen titer: Serial dilutions of plasma are added to thrombin with detection of the last dilution at which plasma is clotted.

•Normal titer: 1/28.

•Causes of low titers: Hypofibrinogenaemia, fibrin degradation products and hyperfibrinolysis. Differentiation is made by repetition of the test after adding: a-Epsilon amino caproic acid: correction means hyperfibrinolysis. b-Saline and protamine sulphate: correction means presence of fibrin degradation products. 67

Original page 68

D-Immunologic methods as ELISA and radio-immunoassays or electrophoresis but these methods gives no idea about the function. E-Gravimetric assay which is based on the weight of the clot:

–Clot weight method: clauss technique is performed, then the clot is compressed, washed, dried and is weighed.

–Clottable protein method: clauss technique is performed, then the clot is dissolved in an alkaline solution followed by spectrophotometric protein measurement.

Thrombin time:

•Method: Patient platelet poor plasma is added to thrombin followed by measurement of the clotting time.

•Normal range: 15-19 seconds. Prolongation of 2 sec more than the control is significant and prolongation 20 seconds or more is definitely abnormal.

Causes of prolongation

1-Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. 2-Afibrinogenemia. 3-Hypofibrinogenemia. 4-Dysfibrinogenemia. 5-Fibrin degradation products. 6-Liver diseases. 7-Extremely prolonged with the use of fractionated heparin or overdose of low molecular weight heparin. 8-Hypoalbuminemia causes in-vitro prolongation. 9-Paraproteinemia. 10-High concentrations of fibrinogen which can inhibit fibrin assembly and can be corrected by dilution of the plasma. 68

Original page 69

Mixing experiments using thrombin time

–Mixing with saline: Neutralizes the hyperfibrinogenemia and paraproteinemia.

–Mixing with normal plasma:Neutralizes hypofibrinogenemia and afibrinogenemia.

–Mixing with the Protamine sulphate: Neutralizes heparin and fibrin degradation products.

–Mixing with the Toluidine blue: Neutralizes heparin and dysfibrinogenemia but not fibrin degradation products.

–Mixing with serum and albumin: Neutralizes the Hypoalbuminemia.

Reptilase (Ancrod) time:

•Thrombin time is performed with adding Reptilase or Ancrod which is extracted from a snake venom instead of thrombin. Reptilase is not inhibited by heparin.

–Correction of the time means presence of heparin or low molecular weight heparin.

–Incorrection of the time means the presence of fibrin degradation products, hypofibrinogenaemia, dysfibrinogenaemia or liver disease. 69

Measurement of the level of coagulation factors: Measurement of themount and not the function using an immunological method as radio-immunoassays, radial immune diffusion or ELISA. 1-Parallel line bioassay of coagulation factors: Measurement of the function and not the amount:

–Serial dilution of both patient and control plasma are made.

–Mixing each dilution of both patient and control plasma 1:1 with plasma deficient in a particular factor.

Laboratory assessment of fibrinolytic system:

1-Fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products (FDPs). 2-D-dimer. 3-Fibrin monomers. 4-Euglobulin lysis test. 5-Lysis of fibrin plate. 6-Venous occlusion test. 7-Measurement of plasminogen. 8-Measurement of plasminogen activator. 9-Measurement of plasminogen activator inhibitor.

Fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products (FDPs):

•Methods: Immunological methods using specific antibodies to the purified D and E fragments.

•Normal range: Less than 10 g/ml.

Causes of raised level of serum FDPs

–DIC “Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy”.

–Streptokinase therapy.

–Thrombosis.

–Myocardial infarction.

–Severe pneumonia.

–After major surgeries.

Detection of D-dimer:

–The same as FDPs test but can be performed on plasma.

–It is a good negative giving except with anticoagulant therapy.

–False positive results may occur in old age, hemolysis, positive rheumatoid factor, lipemia or hyperbilirubinemia. 74

Original page 75

Euglobulin lysis test:

–Platelet poor plasma is mixed with acid in a glass test tube leading to precipitation of the euglobulinfraction which contains factor VIII, fibrinogen, plasminogen activator

–The test tube is checked every ten minutes for complete lysis.

–Normal time of lysis is 90 – 240 min.

–Short lysis occurs in Factor XIII deficiency.

–Prolonged lysis occurs in:

➢Myocardial infarction.

➢Post-operative situations.

➢Thrombosis.

➢Obesity.

➢Last trimester of pregnancy.

Lysis of fibrin plate:

–Diluted fibrinogen is put in a petri dish.

–Thrombin and calcium chloride are added.

–Incubation for 20 minutes for yielding euglobulin. 0

–Incubation at 37C for 24 hours.

–Recording the zone of lysis which is proportional to the level of plasminogen activator. 2

–The normal zone of lysis: 40 - 60 mm.

Venous occlusion test:

–Measurement of the lysis in 2 samples; one sample without venous stasis and the other after sphygmomanometer cuff inflation to a pressure between systole and diastole for 10 min. Normally, the post-occlusion time is 30 min less than the pre-occlusion time. 75

–Failure to enhance lysis occurs in:

➢Thrombosis.

Laboratory diagnosis of Factor XIII deficiency:

1-Clot solubility test :

•Principle: Fibrin clot formed in the presence of Factor XIII is stable for at least 1 hour in 5 mol/1 urea while in the absence of Factor XIII, clot resolves rapidly. The test is more sensitive when the sample is clotted by thrombin.

•Method: Patient plasma is mixed with an equal volume of 10 NIH (National Institute of Health) unit thrombin solution and is incubated for 20 minutes at 0 37C and the urea solution is added with a careful dislodgement of the clot and 0 then is left undisturbed for 24 hours at 37C with inspection at regular intervals.

•Interpretation: The test is abnormal if the clot is resolved after 24 hours. 2-Immunological assays. 76

Original page 77

Platelet Disorders

Megakaryocytosis

•Definition: Increased megakaryocytes in the bone marrow.

Causes

i-Clonal:

–Essential thrombocythemia: Differentiated by the WHO diagnostic criteria.

–Polycythemia vera: Differentiated by the WHO diagnostic criteria.

–Chronic myeloid leukemia: Differentiated by the positive Philadelphia chromosome or BCR-ABL fusion gene.

–Primary myelofibrosis: Differentiated by the WHO diagnostic criteria.

–Myelodysplastic syndrome with (5q-) syndrome or efractory anemia with ring siderob lasts and thrombocytosis (RARA-T): Differentiated from essential thrombocythemia by the presence of dysplasia and by cytogenetics.

–Acute myeloblastic leukemia M7 or with inv(3) or t(3;3) (q21;q26.2) (RPN1- EVI1): Differentiated from essential thrombocythemia by blast count 20% or more in the peripheral blood or bone marrow and by cytogenetics.

ii-Non-clonal:

–Immune thrombocytopenic purpura: Smooth megakaryocytes without budding or separation in the bone marrow, thrombocytopenia in peripheral blood and positive anti-platelet antibodies.

–Hypersplenism: Hyperplasia of megakaryocytes with normal morphology in the bone marrow and pancytopenia in the peripheral blood.

–Drugs causing platelet destruction: History of drug intake, normal morphology of megakaryocytes and thrombocytopenia.

–Bleeding: History of bleeding, anemia and reticulocytosis.

–Infection: Fever, high ESR, positive CRP and positive cultures. 77

Original page 78

Thrombocytosis

•Definition: Increased platelet count in the peripheral blood.

Causes

1-Clonal thrombocytosis:

–Essential thrombocythemia: Differentiated by the WHO diagnostic criteria.

–Polycythemia vera: Differentiated by the WHO diagnostic criteria.

–Chronic myeloid leukemia: Differentiated by the positive Philadelphia chromosome or BCR-ABL fusion gene.

–Primary myelofibrosis: Differentiated by the WHO diagnostic criteria.

–Myelodysplastic syndrome with (5q-) syndrome or efractory anemia with ring siderob lasts and thrombocytosis (RARA-T): Differentiated from essential thrombocythemia by the presence of dysplasia and by cytogenetics.

–Acute myeloblastic leukemia M7 or with inv(3) or t(3;3) (q21;q26.2) (RPN1- EVI1): Differentiated from essential thrombocythemia by blast count 20% or more in the peripheral blood or bone marrow and by cytogenetics. 2-Non-clonal thrombocytosis: Differentiated by presence of a primary cause as:

–Exercise.

–Iron deficiency.

–Drugs as epinephrine.

–Bleeding.

–Hemolysis.

–Post-operative.

–Trauma.

–Infection.

–Inflammation.

–Malignancy. 78

Original page 79

3-Familial thrombocytosis: Autosomal dominant mutation of thrombopoietin gene. 4-Spurious thrombocytosis: False high platelet count due to:

–Severe microcytosis.

–Fragmented red cells.

–Cryoglobulinemia.

–Cytoplasmic fragmentation in leukemia.

–Bacteria. 79

Original page 80

Thrombocytopenia

•Definition: It is a condition characterized by an abnormally low platelet count in the peripheral blood below the low level of normal.

•Severity: Mild (100-150X10/L), Moderate (50-100X10/L) and Marked (< 50X10/L). 999

Causes

I-Congenital Inherited thrombocytopenia:

–Inherited thrombocytopenia with low platelet size.

–Inherited thrombocytopenia with normal platelet size.

–Inherited thrombocytopenia with high platelet size.

II-Congenital non-inherited thrombocytopenia:

–Maternal drugs and chemical agents.

–Isoimmune thrombocytopenia.

–Infiltration of bone marrow.

–Congenital infections.

–Maternal immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

–Maternal disorders.

–Giant cavernous hemangioma.

III-Acquired thrombocytopenia:

1-Decreased production:

–Bone marrow infiltration.

–Infection: HIV or TORCH infection.

–Radiotherapy.

–Deficiency of vitamin B12 or folate.

–Acquired aplastic anemia.

–Acquired pure megakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.

–Myelodysplastic syndrome.

–Myelofibrosis.

–Drugs as Thiazide. 80

Original page 81

2-Increased destruction:

i-Immunological causes: A-Autoimmune thrombocytopenia:

a-Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

b-Secondary immune thrombocytopenia:

–Lymphoproliferative disorders.

–Autoimmune diseases as SLE or rheumatoid arthritis.

–Organ specific autoimmunity

–Evan’s syndrome

–Underlying immune dysregulation syndromes such as Common Variable Immunodeficiency syndrome.

–Infection as HIV

–Post bone marrow transplantation

–Lymphoproliferative disorders. c-Cyclic thrombocytopenia: in young adult female related to menstruation. It may cured spontaneously or progress to bone marrow failure. B-Alloimmune thrombocytopenia: Post-transfusion or transplantation. C-Drug induced immune thrombocytopenia. ii-Non-immunological causes:

A-Thrombocytopenia caused by an increased platelet destruction:

–Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

–Hemolytic uremic syndrome.

–Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.

–Artificial valves.

–Hemophagocytosis

–Snake venoms

–Severe burn 81

Original page 82

B-Thrombocytopenia caused by platelet Sequestration:

–Splenomegaly.

–Hemangioma.

–Hypothermia. C-Thrombocytopenia caused by drugs: Aspirin or Digitoxin. D-Dilutional thrombocytopenia: as in massive blood transfusion.

Approach to diagnosis of thrombocytopenia

I-History:

1-Family history of thrombocytopenia: hereditary causes. 2-Patient history: Recent travels to an infested area by special parasite as malaria. 3-Present history and profile of the thrombocytopenia or of the bleeding. 4-Medical history: Autoimmune disorders, infections, malignancies and pregnancy. 5- Medication history: Recent medications and vaccinations. 6-History of recent transfusions, recent organ transplantation. 7-Diet history: Alcohol intake, quinine-containing beverages, dietary habits.

II-Physical examination:

1-Location and severity of bleeding: Mucocutaneous bleeding. 2-Organomegaly. 3-Skeletal abnormalities. 4-Ischemic limb of skin necrosis: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia thrombosis.

III-Laboratory investigations:

➢Basic laboratory tests: 1-Complete blood count:All the three blood lineages should be assessed. 2-Blood film: A-Platelets are examined for:

–Platelet clumps: To exclude pseudothrombocytopenia.

–Platelet size and granularity. 82

Original page 83

B-White blood cells are examined for:

–Blast cells in acute leukemia.

–Leukocytes abnormalities:

○Pelger Heut anomaly in myelodysplastic syndrome.

○Hypersegmentation in megaloblastic anemia.

○Toxic granulation in sepsis.

○Reactive lymphocytes in viral infection.

○Dohle bodies in May Hagglen anomaly. C-Red blood corpuscles are examined for:

–Schistocytes in thrombotic microangiopathy.

–Microspherocytes in Evan’s syndrome.

–Ovalomacrocytes in megaloblastic anemia,

–Normoblastemia in hemolytic anemia, myelofibrosis and BM infiltration.

–Intracellular parasites in malaria. 3-Liver and renal function tests. 4-Coagulation screen and D-dimer. 5-Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).

➢Second line investigations:According to results of the first line. e.g.: 1-Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy: For exclusion of bone marrow disorders. 2-Reticulated platelets or the equivalent immature platelet fraction: They decrease in thrombocytopenia due to bone marrow failure and increase in hyperdestructive thrombocytopenia. 83

Original page 84

Congenital Platelet Disorders

Etiology

I-Congenital Thrombocytopenia: 1-Congenital non- inherited thrombocytopenia:

–Maternal drugs and chemical agents

–Isoimmune thrombocytopenia

–Infiltration of bone marrow

–Infections

–Maternal immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

–Maternal disorders.

–Giant cavernous hemangioma. 2-Congenital inherited thrombocytopenia:

–Congenital thrombocytopenia with low platelet size.

–Congenital thrombocytopenia with normal platelet size.

–Congenital thrombocytopenia with high platelet size. II-Congenital thrombocytopathy: 1-Defective platelet adhesion. 2-Defective platelet aggregation. 3-Defective platelet signal transduction. 4-Abnormal platelet cytoskeleton. 5-Abnormal platelet Calcium mobilization. 6-Motreal platelet syndrome. 7-Transcriptional factors mutations. 84

Original page 85

Congenital Non - inherited Thrombocytopenia

Maternal Drugs: improves rapidly with a rare severe hemorrhage. Mechanisms: 1-Decreased platelet production, as with ethanol, thiazides, chlorpropamide, tolbutamide, estrogens, steroids, alkylating agents, antimetabolites or chemotherapeutic drugs. 2-Damaging platelets either directly or through the formation of platelet antibodies as in quinine, quinidine, hydralazine or some antibiotics. Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia: Definition:Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia is a neonatal thrombocytopenia due to the transfer of maternal platelet allo-antibodies to the fetus. Mechanism:

–Mother is negative for certain platelet antigens + Foetus is positive for that antigen → Antigen passes to maternal circulation → Active immunization of the mother → Formation of antibodies against this antigen → Placental transfer after 14 weeks of gestation → Immune mediated destruction of foetus’s platelet after 20 weeks of gestation.

–The first pregnancy is affected with 80% recurrence in incompatible foetuses.

–Causative antigens: 80% of cases are caused by human platelet antigen-1 (HPA-1), 15% by HPA-5b antigen and 5% by other platelet specific antibodies.

–Type of antibodies: Initially IgM (can’t cross placenta) and then, IgG (cross placenta).

–Severity of thrombocytopenia depends on:

○Maternal IgG concentration and subclass.

○The density of the target antigen on the fetal platelets.

○Fetal reticulo-endothelial system.

○Fetal bone marrow compensation ability.

Clinical picture

a-Petechiae and purpura, or more severe bleeding at the time of birth. b-Severe bleeding within the first week and improvement within one month but severe and fatal intracranial hemorrhages may occur. 85

Original page 86

Laboratory diagnosis

1-Daily Cord complete blood count: Thrombocytopenia. 2-Serology:

–Identifying platelet antigens in mother, father and foetus.

–Antibodies in mother’s serum against antigens of both father and foetus platelets.

Treatment

I-Foetal management:

1-The condition is self-limited and is usually corrected within 15-28 days. 2-Platelet transfusion:

–The most preferable: Compatible antigen free platelets or platelets from the mother after removal of the plasma and suspension in saline.

–Less preferably, exchange transfusion is performed.

–Emergency cases: Random platelets under the coverage of IVIg. II-Maternal management: IV Ig, corticosteroids and elective CS 2-4 weeks before term. Bone marrow infiltration: Extremely rare. E.g.: disseminated reticuloendotheliosis, congenital leukaemia, solid tumors, myelofibrosis, Gaucher’s disease, Niemann–Pick disease and the mucopolysaccharidosis. Congenital infections: Maternal TORCH infection or vaccinations. Mechanisms: a-Decreased production due to invasion of megakaryocytes. b-Destruction of the circulating platelets. c-Immune complexes deposition on the surface of platelets. Maternal ITP: Maternal auto-antibodies cross the placenta. Maternal disorders: as pre-eclampsia, systemic lupus erythymatosus or other autoimmune diseases, especially if the woman has anti-phospholipid antibodies. Giant cavernous hemangioma: Consumption of platelets within the tumour. 86

Original page 87

Congenital Inherited Thrombocytopenia

Inherited thrombocytopenias with reduced platelet size:

1-Wiskott – Aldrich syndrome (WAS): It is a rare X-linked recessive disease characterized by eczema, thrombocytopenia and immunodeficiency.

•Etiology: Mutation ofWiskott – Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) gene.

•Clinical picture:

–Age of presentation: the first months of life and usually before the age of 3 years.

–Mild intermittent bleeding and bloody diarrhea.

–Susceptibility to infections.

–Eczema.

–Death at an early age due to intracranial haemorrhage, infection or lymphoreticular malignancy.

•Laboratory investigations:

–Complete blood picture: Marked thrombocytopenia and Absolute eosinophilia.

–Blood film: Decreased platelet size.

–Decreased platelet survival.

–Bleeding time: Prolonged.

–Platelet aggregometry: Decreased platelet aggregation and release.

–Flowcytometry: Defects in cellular immunity (↓ CD8+ lymphocytes).

–Serology: Decreased humoral immunity (↓ serum IgM, ↑ serum IgA and IgE).

–Genetic tests.

•Treatment:

–Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

–Gene therapy.

–Splenectomy prolongs the platelet life-span. 2-X-linked thrombocytopenia: Mutation of WAS gene with isolated thrombocytopenia. 87

Original page 88

Inherited thrombocytopenia with normal platelet size:

1-Thrombocytopenia with absent radii (TAR) syndrome:

•Inheritance: Autosomal recessive inheritance.

•Etiology and pathogenesis:Thrombopoietin signalling defect.

•Clinical picture:

–Severe bleeding that starts during infancy.

–Skeletal abnormalities: Bilateral agenesis of the radius, absent ulna and humerus or other skeletal abnormalities.

–Structural malformations of the heart, and kidney.

•Laboratory investigations:

–Complete blood picture: Leukomoid reaction and thrombocytopenia.

–Bone marrow: Decreased megakaryocytes and dysmegakaryopoiesis.

2-Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (CAMT):

•Inheritance: Autosomal recessive inheritance.

•Etiology:Mutations of the HOXA11 → Thrombopoitin receptor (cMPL) defect.

•Clinical picture:

–Expressed in infancy and identified within a few days or the first month of birth.

–Proximal radio - ulnar synostosis, syndactyly and other skeletal abnormalities.

–Causes of death: Fatal infections or hemorrhages.

•Complications: Complete aplasia of the bone marrow as the cMPL is also required for stem cell maturation.

•Laboratory investigations: 9

–Complete blood count: Marked thrombocytopenia (< 10X10/L).

–Bone marrow: Absence of megakaryocytes.

–Serum thrombopoietin level: Elevated.

•Treatment: The only effective treatment is the platelet transfusion. 88

Original page 89

3-Schulman – Upshaw syndrome:

•Etiology: Autosomal recessive mutation in ADAMTS13 gene.

•Clinical presentation: Neonatal TTP with frequent relapses, and response to fresh plasma infusion.

•Laboratory investigations:

–Complete blood picture: Anemia and thrombocytopenia.

–Blood film: Fragmented red blood corpuscles.

–Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) enzyme: Increased.

–Serum ADAMTS-13: Less than 5%.

4-Fanconi’s anemia.

5-Chediak-Hegashi syndrome.

89

Original page 90

Inherited thrombocytopenias with increased platelet size (The commonest):

1-May –Hegglin anomaly: Uncommon Autosomal dominant mutations of the MYH9 encoding the non-muscle myosin heavy chain peptide-IIA →. Affection of the assembly and stability of myosin → Defective platelet and leucocyte structure and functions.

•Clinical picture: Infrequent Bleeding with no increased susceptibility to infection.

•Laboratory investigations: a-CBC: Mild to marked thrombocytopenia and mild neutropenia. b-Blood film: Giant hyopogranular platelets and Dohle bodies in granulocytes. c-BM: Defective megakaryocyte maturation with bizarre morphology and hypergranularity and Döhle bodies in granulocytes. 2-Sebastian, Fetchner and Epstein syndromes: Uncommon autosomal dominant mutations of the MYH9 gene → Absent or clumped non-muscle myosin heavy chain- IIA protein and failure of shape changes.

•Clinical picture: Sensori-neural hearing loss, cataract and glomerulonephritis.

•Laboratory investigations: Thrombocytopenia with giant platelets and Döhle bodies in granulocytes. 3-Grey platelet syndrome (GPS): Autosomal dominant defect in NBEAL2 gene → Defect in maturation and packing of α granules during megakaryocytic differentiation → Leakage of their contents into plasma, lungs and bone marrow during megakaryocytic migration. It may be associated with myelofibrosis. Autosomal recessive or X-linked inheritance has been shown.

•Clinical picture: Mild to moderate bleeding due to: ↓ Content of α granules and ↓ platelet number and survival.

•Laboratory investigations: a-CBC: Mild to moderate thrombocytopenia. 90

Original page 91

b-Blood film: Giant grey ghost like oval platelets with platelet anisocytosis and abnormal neutrophil granules c-Platelet aggregometry: Moderately decreased or even normal platelet aggregation. d-Decreased platelet survival. e-Platelet granular contents: Decreased number and content of α granules as fibrinogen, Von Willebrand factor, thrombospondin, β thromboglobulin and platelet factor 4 with normal plasma β thromboglobulin. f-Bone marrow: There may be signs of myelofibrosis. . 4-Mediterranean macrothrombocytopenia: heterozygous pattern of the autosomal dominant Bernard-Soulier syndrome. 5-Pseudo-Von Willebrand disease: Autosomal dominant mutation in GPIb → ↑ Binding to VWF → VWF consumption.

–Complete blood count: Thrombocytopenia.

–Blood film: Large platelet.

–RIPA (Ristocetin induced platelet aggregation):

▪Washed platelets of the patient + Cryorecipitate → Spontaneous aggregation.

▪Washed donor platelets + Patient plasma → No spontaneous aggregation.

▪Patient platelet rich plasma + low dose of ristocetin (0.5 mg/ml) → Exagerated response.

–Treatment: Platelet concentrate. 6-Jacobsen syndrome and Paris– Troussau syndrome: Autosomal dominant deletion of FLI1 gene → Dysmegakaryopiesis → Thrombocytopenia → Mild bleeding.

7-Bernard – Soulier syndrome.

8-Stomatocytosis.

91

Original page 92

Congenital Thrombocytopathies

Disorders of platelet adhesion:

1-Bernard – Soulier syndrome. 2-Pseudo Von Willebrand disease. 3-Defective GPIaIIIa (binding to collagen). Bernard – Soulier syndrome: Rare autosomal recessive quantitative and qualitative abnormalities of GPIb α, GPIX and GPIbβ → Defective binding to Von Willebrand factor → Defective platelet adhesion. A dominant transmission had been recorded.

•Clinical picture: Mild to severe bleeding out of proportion to platelet count and fatal hemorrhage is rare.

Laboratory investigations

9

–CBC: Variable thrombocytopenia from 10 – 20 X 10 to near normal.

–Blood film: Giant platelets and platelet pseudonucleus.

–Bone marrow: Normal megakaryocytes.

–Bleeding time is prolonged and Hess test is ositive.

–Platelet adhesion: Less than 25 %.

–Platelet function analyser-100 (PFA-100): Abnormal results.

–Platelet coagulant activity: Decreased.

–Platelet aggregometry:

○Absent agglutination with ristocetin not corrected by the adding normal plasma.

○Delayed aggregation with thrombin.

○Normal aggregation with other aggregating agents.

–Platelet granules and secretion study: Normal ATP secretion

–Platelet thromboxane B2 formation: Normal.

–Clot retraction: Normal.

–Flowcytometry: Decreased expression of CD 42.

•Treatment: Platelet transfusion is required in severe bleeding episodes. 92

Original page 93

Disorders of platelet aggregation:

1-Defective primary aggregation. 2-Defective secondary aggregation. Defects of primary aggregation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GT): Rare autosomal recessive quantitative or qualitative abnormalities of GPIIb/IIIa. There are three types:

–Type I: Severe deficiency (< 5%) → Marked ↓ Platelet aggregation and clot retraction.

–Type II(10 – 20%): Platelet microaggregates and moderate impairment of clot retraction.

–Type II: The GPIIb/IIIa is more than 50% of the normal. N.B.:The GPIIb/IIIa is needed for fibrinogen uptake from plasma and storage in alpha granules.

•Clinical picture: Extremely variable from mild to severe easy and spontaneous bruising, mucosal bleeding, subcutaneous hematoma and petechiae. Hemarthrosis is rare and fatal hemorrhages may occur.

Laboratory investigations

–Complete blood count: Normal platelet count.

–Blood film: Normal platelet morphology.

–Coagulation times: Normal.

–Bleeding time is prolonged and Hess test is positive.

–Platelet adhesion: Decreased.

–Platelet function analyser-100 (PFA-100): Abnormal.

–Platelet aggregometry: ↓ Aggregation with epinephrine, ADP and collagen with normal response to ristocetin.

–Clot retraction: Impaired or absent.

–Platelet coagulant activity: Decreased.

–Flowcytometry: ↓ Expression of CD41 and CD61 < 5% of normal.

–Platelet fibrinogen content: Decreased.

•Management: Platelet transfusion in severe bleeding. 93

Original page 94

Defects of secondary aggregation:

a-Storage pool deficiency. b-Quebec platelet syndrome. c-Selective impairment of the thromboxane A2 receptor. Storage pool deficiency (SPD):Very rare heterogeneous disorders which may be caused by deficiency of alpha granules only (Grey platelet syndrome), deficiency of delta granules only or deficiency of both granules.

Inheritance

–Autosomal dominant.

–Autosomal recessive in storage pool disease associated with:

○Thrombocytopenia with absent radii (TAR) syndrome.

○Hermansky – Pudlak syndrome (HPS).

○Chédiak– Higashi syndrome.

–X-linked in storage pool disease associated with Wiskott-Alderich syndrome.

Laboratory investigations

–Platelet aggregometry: Absent ADP and adrenaline induced secondary aggregation waves and normal ristocetin induced aggregation.

–Platelet granules study: Severe or partial granule deficiency.

–Electron microscopy: Deficiency of dense bodies 14

–Decreased ADP and ATP measurement by lumiaggregometry, HPLC and C serotonin release assay. Hermansky – Pudlak syndrome:Autosomal recessive mutation of 8 genes (HPS 1-8) → Abnormal intracellular vesicles → Mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding, oculocutaneous albinism, pulmonary fibrosis and inflammatory bowel. Chédiak– Higashi syndrome:Autosomal recessive mutation of CHS1/LYST gene → Mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding, oculocutaneous albinism increased susceptibility to infections and fatal lympho-histiocytic infiltration. 94

Original page 95

ADP receptors defects:It is a very rare autosomal recessive defect.

•P2Y 1 ADP receptor: Impaired platelet aggregation and clot retraction.

•P2Y 12 ADP receptor: Shape change with blunted aggregation.

•P2X ADP receptor defect: Its actual rule is not fully understood.

Diagnosis:

❖Clinical diagnosis: Lifelong history of mucocutaneous bleeding and excessive postsurgical or post traumatic blood loss.

❖Screening test: Failure of full irreversible platelet aggregation by ADP, even at very high concentrations (>10 μM).

❖Confirmatory tests:

➢Inability of ADP to inhibit the increase of platelet levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate after the exposure of platelets to prostaglandin E1 or other stimuli for adenylyl cyclase.

➢Inability of ADP to inhibit the phosphorylation of vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein after the exposure of platelets to prostaglandin E1 or other stimuli for adenylyl cyclase.

❖Molecular identification of the defect. 95

Original page 96

Neonatal thrombocytopenia

•Definition: Neonatal thrombocytopenia is defined as a neonatal platelet count below the low limit of the reference range for age.

Etiology

1-Fetal thrombocytopenia: Presented at birth. It may be due to:

❖Allo-immune thrombocytopenia.

❖Congenital Infection as cytomegalovirus, toxoplasma, rubella and HIV.

❖Inherited thrombocytopenia as Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.

❖Aneuploidy as trisomies 18, 13, 21, or triploidy. 2-Early-onset thrombocytopenia:Presented during the first 3 days. It is caused by:

❖Chronic intra-uterine hypoxia due to placental insufficiency.

❖Acute perinatal hypoxia.

❖Small-for-gestational-age: Caused by chronic hypoxia.

❖Perinatal bacterial infection as E.coli, group B streptococci or hemophilus influenza: It is rare cause of early-onset neonatal thrombocytopenia.

❖Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.

❖Maternal auto-immune diseases as ITP and SLE.

❖Allo-immune thrombocytopenia. 3-Late-onset thrombocytopenia: Presented after the first 3 l days. It is caused by:

❖Systemic bacterial late onset sepsis.

❖Necrotising enterocolitis.

Pathogenesis

–Decreased platelet production (The most common): Genetic causes and causes of bone marrow infiltration or suppression.

–Increased platelet destruction or consumption: Immunological or non- immunological.

–Combined increased platelet destruction and decreased platelet production. 96

Original page 97

Approach to neonatal thrombocytopenia

I-History:

❖Family history: Positive in inherited cases.

❖Maternal history:

–History of medication.

–History of transfusion.

–History of travel to an endemic area.

–History of autoimmue diseases.

–History of malignant diseases.

–History of infection or vaginal colonization with group B beta hemolytic streptococci.

–History of immune thrombocytopenic purpura.

–Blood group and Rh

❖Neonatal history:

–History of prematurity or low birth weight.

–History of admission to nenatal intensive care unit.

–History of sepsis.

–History of medication.

–Bleeding history.

–Blood group and Rh.

II-Physical examination:

❖Location and severity of bleeding:

–Hemorrhage, purpura, or other signs of severe thrombocytopenia is uncommon except in neonatal alloimmune or autoimmune thrombocytopenia and some inherited thrombocytopenias.

–Fetal thrombocytopenia may be as severe as it may be presented with intracranial hemorrhage. 97

Original page 98

–The presence of joint or extensive soft tissue bleeding suggests the presence of coagulation abnormalities, such as occurs in DIC.

❖Skeletal abnormalities: Common with inherited cases.

❖Hemangioma.

III-Laboratory evaluation:

❖Complete blood count:

–Thrombocytopenia.

–MPV is normal when thrombocytopenia is caused by reduced production, and elevated when it is caused by accelerated destruction.

–Anemia in hemorrhage or DIC.

–Leukocytosis, absolute neutrophilia and absolute monocytosis in sepsis or absolute lymphocytosis in viral infections.

❖Blood film: The three hematological lineages are examined carefully:

–Exclusion of pseudothrombocytopenia.

–Platelet morphology as the presence of giant platelet or hypogranulated platelets (ghost platelets).

–Shistocytes in DIC.

–Spherocytes in severe Rh disease.

–Normoblastemia in neonatal hypoxia.

–White blood cells inclusions in inherited thrombocytopenia.

–Neutrophilic left shift, toxic granulations and vaculation in sepsis.

❖Reticulated platelets is low when platelet production is low and high when platelets are being consumed at an accelerated rate.

❖Thrombopoietin is high when platelet production is low.

❖Bone marrow Examination:

–Megakaryocytes: Few megakaryocytes with low platelet production, and many megakaryocytes with accelerated platelet destruction.

–Infiltration by malignancy. 98

Original page 99

❖Arterial blood gases: This may show hypoxia.

❖Fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products: High in DIC.

❖Serology:

–Immune thrombocytopenia: Identifying platelets antigens in mother, father and fetus and identifying maternal anti- platelets antibodies which are directed against father and fetus platelets antigens.

–Viral antibodies.

❖Karyotyping: may detect anaeploidy.

❖Metabolic screening: May detect aminoaciduria.

Management

–Platelet transfusion guidelines are: 9

➢Platelet count (< 30X10/L): Platelet transfusion. 9

➢Platelet count (30-49X10/L): Transfusion in the following conditions:

○Weight is less than 1000g and age less than 7 days.

○Clinical instability.

○Previous major bleeding.

○Currant minor bleeding.

○Concurrent coagulopathy.

○Requiring surgery or exchange transfusion. 9

➢Platelet count (50-99X10/L): Platelet transfusion only if there is bleeding. 9

➢Platelet count (> 99X10/L): No transfusion.

–Red blood cell transfusion in severe anemia.

–Treatment of the cause: e.g.:

○Corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulins in immune causes.

○Fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate in DIC.

○Antibiotics in sepsis.

○Correction of the hypoxia. 99
