Acquired Thrombocytopenia

Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP)

•Definition: Acquired autoimmune disorder of isolated thrombocytopenia with platelet 9 count <100X10/L, normal BM and absence of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

•Pathogenesis: loss of tolerance to self-antigen caused by: I-Dysregulation of the immune response in the form of: A-Auto-antibodies that causes opsonization:

○Type of antibodies: IgG in most common but may be IgA or IgM

○Target antigen is either in megakaryocytes or platelets: 1-Megakaryocytes leading to: Inhibition of growth, development and release of platelets or induction of apoptosis. 2-Platelets: GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb-IX-V complex in most cases but may be GPIa/IIIa or GPVI.

○Role of spleen: Source of antibodies and site of sensitization and destruction.

B-T-cell dysregulation:

+

–Direct CD8 T-cell mediated cytotoxicity and impairment of platelet production.

–Decreased Treg populations which leads to loss of tolerance.

–Abnormal cytokine profiles.

–Altered Th1/Th2 balance.

II-H.pylori infection:

–Antibodies against H.pylori → Bind to the FC receptors → activate platelet or interact with H.pylori bound VWF and platelet GPIb.

–Somatic mutation of antibodies → Second-generation cross-react with platelets.

–Additional somatic mutation → Third-generation react only against platelets. III-Impairment of megakaryopoiesis: This is evident by:

–Abnormal appearance by electron microscope and aabnormal growth in tissue cultures.

–The minimally elevated thrombopoietin level.

IV-Increased platelet clearance by the Ashwell-Morrell receptor system in the liver.

V-Specific genetic determinants:e.g.: MHC polymorphism. 100

Original page 101

Clinical picture

1-Bleeding: It is unusual with no correlation between platelet count and bleeding because of the good function of giant platelets and because giant platelets may cause a falsely lower count in the automated machines. 9

–< 20X10/L: Purpura, petechiae “dependent regions” or mucosal bleeding. 9

–< 10X10/L: Spontaneous hematoma in the mouth and mucous membranes. 9

–< 5X10/L: Major or fatal bleeding including intracranial or internal bleeding.

2-No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.

3-Clinical types:

a-Acute or childhood type which is characterized by:

–It is common in children with no sex difference.

–It is preceded by a viral infection.

–It has an acute onset.

–It is self-limited but 15% of patients develops the chronic type.

–Phases of acute ITP:

➢Newly diagnosed: Within the first 3 months of diagnosis.

➢Persistent ITP: 3 – 12 months of diagnosis without spontaneous remission or complete response with therapy.

➢Chronic ITP: After 12 months of diagnosis. b-Chronic or adult type which is characterized by:

–It is common in adults between 20-45 years and more common in females.

–It is associated with other autoimmune diseases.

–It has an insidious onset and chronic course of remission and exacerbation.

•Diagnosis: It is a diagnosis of exclusion. The most specific test is the response to ITP treatment: I-History: 1-Patient history: Especially the character and site of bleeding and medication history. 2-Family history: For exclusion of hereditary causes. II-Physical examination: For organo-megaly to exclude other causes. 101

Original page 102

III-Laboratory investigations:

9 1-CBC: Isolated thrombocytopenia < 100X10/L with MPV is high and PDW. 2-Blood film:

–Exclusion of pseudothrombocytopenia.

–Giant platelets with increased reticulated platelets.

–NO fragmented red blood corpuscles. 3-Bleeding time: Prolonged and Coagulation tests:normal 4-Blood group and Rh typing: Blood transfusion may be indicated. 5-DAT is negative.It is performed to exclude Evan’s syndrome. 6-Serum quantitative immunoglobulins: To exclude immune deficiency syndrome. 7-Serology and PCR for H. pylori and viral infection: To exclude the infectious causes. 8-Anti-phospholipid antibodies, antinuclear antibodies and anti-thyroid antibodies: To exclude other autoimmune diseases 9-BM examination: It isn’t recommend because isolated thrombocytopenia is rare to be the only presentation of aplastic anemia or leukemia unless:

▪Treatment failure or relapse.

▪Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy to exclude other causes.

▪Ages more than 60 years to exclude MDS.

▪Before splenectomy.

–Findings:

▪Normal development and maturation of all lines.

▪Normal or ↑ megakaryocytes especially small megakaryocytes. Megakaryocytes are small with absent or decreased platelet separation and budding. 10-Serum complement measurement: Low. 11-Anti-Glycoprotein specific antibodies: Positive. 12-Anti-platelet antibodies: Positive. They are not sensitive or specific. 13-Monoclonal Ab specific immobilization of PLT Ag:90% specific with low sensitivity. 51111 14-Platelet survival studyusing Chromium or Indiuumlabelled platelets: ↓. 102

Original page 103

•Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia “See before”.

•Treatment: The aim of treatment is not the normalization of platelet count but to maintain a safe platelet count which differs from patient to other. Treatment includes:

–Corticosteroids, IVIG, anti-D antibodies and immunosuppressants.

–Splenectomy.

–Thrombopoietin receptor agonists.

•Quality of response: It is determined by two separate measures 7 days apart: 9

–Complete response (CP): Platelet count > 100X10/L with no bleeding. 9

–Response (R): Platelet count > 30X10/L or > 2 fold of the base with no bleeding.

–Time to response: From start of treatment to CR or R. 9

–No response (NR): Platelet count < 30X10/L or < 2 fold of the base with or bleeding.

–Loss of CR or R: 9

▪Platelet count < 100X10/L or there is bleeding after CR. 9

▪Platelet count < 30X10/L or < 2 fold of the base with or bleeding after R.

•Prognosis: Good in children with spontaneous remission during the first 10 years of life.

•Refractory ITP: It is an ITP which fulfill all of the following criteria: 1-Failure to achieve CR or R after splenectomy. 2-Need for treatment. 3-Primary ITP confirmed by exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia.

–Management:

▪Investigation of other possible causes of thrombocytopenia.

▪Treatment:

➢Corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or cyclophosphamide.

➢Rituximab: It is a monoclonal antibody against CD20 of B cells.

➢Combination chemotherapy. 103

Original page 104

Post-transfusion Thrombocytopenia

Post-transfusion thrombocytopenia may be due to: Dilutional, transmitted anti-platelet Abs or post-transfusion allo-immune thrombocytopenia. Post-transfusion Allo-Immune Thrombocytopenia: It is a rare fatal clinical disorder of delayed severe thrombocytopenia caused by platelet allo-Abs one week after blood transfusion.

•Pathogenesis: HPA1a-negative platelets recipient pre-sensitized by previous transfusion or pregnancy + platelet from a donor with HPA1a-positive platelets → anti-HPA1a antibodies by the recipient → destruction of both donor and recipient platelets → immune thrombocytopenia 7-10 days after transfusion. Destruction of platelets occurs through:

–Ab coated platelets are destroyed by complement system or phagocytosed in the RES.

–Immune complex deposition on HPA-1a-positive donor platelets via Fc receptor.

–Immune complex deposition on HPA-1a-negative recipient platelets via Fc receptor.

–Soluble platelet antigen in donor plasma → Adsorped by recipient platelets → Destruction of the recipient platelets by Abs against the donor platelets.

–Cross-reaction of anti-HPA-1a Abs with undefined Ag on HPA-1a negative platelets.

•Clinical picture: Unexplained bruising or bleeding 2 - 14 days after transfusion with 30% showing major bleeding and 10% mortality. If limited, recovery occurs within 21 days.

•Laboratory diagnosis: Marked thrombocytopenia 7-10 days after platelet transfusion with positive IgG against HPA-1a antigen.

•Differential diagnosis: Differential Diagnosis of thrombocytopenia “See before”.

•Treatment: It is self-limited in 1-3 weeks.Severe cases may require:

–Plasmapharesis.

–Corticosteroids and high dose of IVIG.

–Splenectomy.

–HLA matched PLT transfusion of little value because transfused platelets will be destroyed.

–Transfusion to this patient should be autologous or from an Ag matched family member. 104

Original page 105

Drug Induced Immune Thrombocytopenia

•Definition: It is a condition of low platelet count secondary to drug administration

Pathogenesis

1-Hapten- dependent antibodies: As penicillin and some cephalosporins → act as hapten → bindcovalently to the PLT membrane protein → Inducing Ab formation. 2-Quinidine-type drugs: As quinine, sulfonamide and NSAIDs → non-covalent attachment to PLT membrane glycoproteins as GPIb/V/IX or GPIIb/IIIa → conformational changes → antibodies against the neo-epitope. 3-Fiban-type drugs: As tirofiban and eptifiberide → react with GPIIb/IIIa → conformational changes → neo-epitopes. 4-Drug-specific antibodies:Abciximab is a chimeric (mouse/human) Fab fragment of monoclonal Ab for GPIIIa. Pathogenic Abs are directed against the mouse part. 5-Immune complex formation: Heparin attaches to the PF4 → drug-Ag complex → Abs → immune complex → binding to the FC receptors on PLT → PLT activation. 6-Auto-antibodies: As gold salts and procainamide → Abs which react with the body own platelets in the absence of the drug. 7-The most recent theory:Drug-dependent Abs are naturally occurring with weak affinity to self-Ag. Certain drugs strengthen the Ag-Ab interaction → destruction of cells only in the presence of the drug.

•Clinical picture: Abrupt severe bleeding “mucosal bleeding or oral hemorrhagic bullae” with other findings of drug sensitivity as nausea, vomiting, fever and rash.

Diagnosis

I-Clinical diagnosis:Careful drug history to fulfill the diagnostic criteria:

–Criteria: 1-Drug intake precedes the thrombocytopenia and recovery is complete and sustained after discontinuation of the drug. 105

Original page 106

2-The drug is the only drug used before the onset of thrombocytopenia or other drugs are continued or reintroduced after discontinuation of the causative drug with a sustained normal platelet count. 3-Exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia. 4-Re-exposure to the drug results in recurrence.

–Diagnostic levels:

○Level I (Definite diagnosis): All the 4 criteria are fulfilled.

○Level II (Probable diagnosis): The first, second and third criteria are fulfilled.

○Level III (Possible diagnosis): The first criterion is fulfilled.

○Level IV (unlikely diagnosis): The first criterion is not met.

II-Laboratory investigations:

–Complete blood count:

○Severe thrombocytopenia in both EDTA and citrated blood samples 6-7 days after starting the drug or within hours in sensitized patients with complete recovery 7-10 days after stopping of the drug. Weeks or months are required for recovery with gold salts because gold remains in tissues for a long period.

○Leukopenia may be found if there are multiple cell target for the drug- dependent antibodies.

–Blood film: Exclusion of pseudothrombocytopenia. GPIIbIIIa inhibitor can produce platelet aggregates even in the citrated samples.

–Complications as:

○Elevated liver enzymes.

○Impaired renal functions.

○DIC in the form of anemia, thrombocytopenia, fragmented red blood corpuscles in the blood smear and high D-dimer and FDPs.

•Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia “See before”.

•Treatment: Stop of the causative drug with supportive measures. 106

Original page 107

Thrombotic microangiopathy

•Definition: Generalized thrombosis in capillaries and arterioles due to an endothelial cell inury, consumptive thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and end-organ ischemia and infarction affecting particularly the kidney and brain.

Etiology

–Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

–Hemolytic uremic syndrome.

–Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy.

–Renal cortical necrosis and acute glomerulonephritis.

–Malignant hypertension.

–Primary pulmonary hypertension.

–Pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome.

–Systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases.

–Allogenic bone marrow transplantation or solid organ transplantation.

–Polyarteritis nodosa and Wegner’s granulomatosis.

–Cavernous hemangioma (Kasabach-Meritt syndrome).

–Mitomycin C, Cyclosporin or other drugs as qunine, quinidine or ticlopidine.

–Irradiation.

–Cardiac surgery.

–Carcinomatosis: Mucin secreting tumors or AML especially M3.

–Paraproteinemia.

Pathogenesis

–Insults → endothelial cell injury → thrombosis in small blood vessels due to:

○Loss of the physiological anticoagulant mechanisms of the endothelial cells.

○Leukocyte adhesion to the damaged endothelial cells.

○Exposure to sub-endothelial collagen.

○Release of VWF. 107

Original page 108

–Thrombosis inside the small vessels → ↑ vascular shear → platelet aggregation and destruction of red blood corpuscles.

–The abnormal ADAMTS-13 → ↓ fragmentation of VWF.

–Thrombocytopenia is caused by platelet consumption.

–Thrombi are consisted of different amounts of platelets and fibrin:

○TTP: The thrombus is consisted of a lot of platelets and VWF and few fibrin.

○HUS: The thrombus is consisted of few platelets and a lot of fibrin.

Clinical picture

–Fever.

–Clinical picture of thrombocytopenia: Petechae.

–Clinical picture of anemia: Pallor and general weakness.

–Neurological manifestations as transient ischemic attacks and strokes are more common in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

–Renal manifestations are more common in hemolytic uremic syndrome.

–Severe cases are presented with multi-organ failure and may be presented by cardiac or gastrointestinal manifestations.

Laboratory investigations

–Complete blood count: anemia and thrombocytopenia.

–Blood film:

○Fragmented red blood corpuscles more than 1% of red blood corpuscles.

○Polychromasi due to reticulocytosis.

○Thrombocytopenia with giant platelets.

–Coomb’s test is negative. It is performed for exclusion of Evan’s syndrome.

–BM examination shows hyperplasia of megakaryocyte and erythroid lineages.

–Bleeding time is prolonged and Hiss test is positive.

–Coagulation tests are normal and D-dimer and FDPs levels are normal.

–Serum haptoglobin level is less than 10 mg/dl.

–Serum indirect bilirubin: Increased. 108

Original page 109

–Serum LDH level is high. It is elevated due to hemolysis and/or tissue ischemia.

–Free hemoglobin in serum and urine.

–Serum Creatinine is more than 1.5 mg/dl.

–Urine examination shows microalbuminuria, hematuria and red cell casts.

–VWF: The ultra-large VWF is not present in plasma in TTP because it rapidly binds to PLT.

–Serum ADAMTS-13 activity < 10% in TTP.

–Serum complement C3 is low in hemolytic uremic syndrome.

–H factor is abnormal in hemolytic uremic syndrome.

•Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis of causes of anemia and thrombocytopenia:

–TTP: Less renal and more neurological manifestations, prolonged bleeding time, normal coagulation tests, D-dimer and FDPs levels, low levels of ultra-large VWF and ADAMTS13 activity < 10%.

–HUS: Preceded by abloodydiarrhea and is associated with less neurological and more renal manifestations, low serum C3 level and may be an abnormal H factor. ↑ Bleeding time, normal coagulation tests, D-dimer and FDPs levels.

–DIC: Underlying serious medical condition, associated anemia, fragmented RBCs in the blood film, ↑ coagulation tests and positive D-dimer and FDPs.

–Preeclampsia and eclampsia: More renal damage, malignant hypertension, less anemia, less thrombocytopenia and elevated liver enzymes.

–Connective tissue disorders: Less severe clinical affection and thrombosis occurs in the large vessels, positive anti-nuclear antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodioes or lupus like anticoagulants.

–Severe vasculitis: Abnormal Doppler results, abnormal vessel wall biopsy and may be positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies.

–Evan’s syndrome: Positive coomb’s test and absence of neurologic manifestations and fragmented RBCs. Spherocytes and microspherocytes are present in blood film. ↑ Bleeding time, normal coagulation tests, D-dimer and FDPs levels. 109

Original page 110

–Drug-induced thrombocytopenia and anemia: It can be excluded by taking a medication history and absence of drug dependent antibodies.

–Disseminated malignancy: It is characterized by positive tests for metastatic cancers.

–Acute leukemia: Blasts in peripheral blood and/or BM, severe anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, cytogenetic abnormalities, special cytochemistry findings, characteristic immunophenotyping and may be associated with leukocytosis.

–BM infiltration: Leukoerythroblastic reaction and presence of the infiltrates in the BM.

–BM failure: Peripheral blood cytopenia, reticulocytopenia and hypo-cellular BM.

–Megaloblastic anemia: Cytopenia, macrocytois, reticulocytopenia, ovalomacrocytes and, giant bands and hypersegmented neutrophils in the peripheral blood smears, megaloblastic changes in the bone marrow smear and low serum vitamin B12 and folate and low red cell folate with a good response to therapeutic vitamin B12 and folate.

–MDS: Cytopenia, reticulocytopenia, hypercellular BM, dysplastic changes in both peripheral blood and BM and characteristic genetic abnormalities.

–Myelofibrosis: Cytopenia, reticulocytopenia, leukoerythroblastic reaction, replacement of hematopoietic tissues by fibrous tissues, and may be characteristic genetic abnormalities as JAK 2 or cMPL mutations.

–Hypersplenism: Cytopenia, splenomegaly and hyper-cellular BM. The actual diagnosis is made by radiological finding that the spleen is the site of blood cells destruction.

–Hemophagocytosis: Splenomegaly, fever, cytopenia, reticulocytopenia, high TG and ferritin, low plasma fibrinogen and hemophagocytosis in both peripheral blood and BM. 110

Original page 111

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP): Widespread microvascular thrombosis involving capillaries and arterioles of the brain and other organs.

Types and etiology

1-Acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura:It is the most common type and is more common in adult females. It results from either drugs as ticlopidine, defective immune regulation or HIV infection → auto-Abs formation against ADAMTS-13 which inhibit the proteolytic activity of ADAMTS-13 or enhance its clearance. Antibodies are commonly of the IgG type but may be of IgA or IgM. 2-Congenital thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura: It results from an autosomal recessive homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation of ADAMTS-13 → ↓ ADAMTS-13 synthesis, intracellular trafficking, secretion or proteolytic activity.

•Pathogenesis: Pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before”.

•Clinical picture: Clinical picture of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before”.

•Laboratory investigations: Investigations of thrombotic microangiopathy “see befor”.

•Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before”.

Treatment

1-Plasma exchange: This decreases the ultra-large VWF and the auto-Abs and give ADAMTES 13 to decrease mortality from 90% to 10%. 2-Splenectomy. 3-Drugs as: Pridnisone, immunospressants, IVIG and monoclonal anti CD20 Abs. 4-Immunoadsorption: To staphylococcal protein A. 111

Original page 112

Hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS): Thrombosis, mainly in the renal vessels, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and renal affection.

Types and etiology

I-Typical or Diarrhea related type: It represents about 90% of cases:

–It is caused by infection by E coli O157 H7 and less commonly by Shigella dysentriae serotype 1 → release verotoxin, shigatoxin or shiga-like exotoxin → thrombosis in the small vessels especially in those of the kidney through:

○Binding to globotriaosylceramide 3 membrane receptor abundant in the glomerular capillary endothelial cells → toxin-receptor complex → endocytosis → cytolysis and extensive endothelial cell injury.

○Activation of the alternative pathway of the complement.

○Binding to GPIIa of the platelet causing platelet activation.

○Inhibition of Elongation factor-1 (EF-1) leading to inhibition of protein synthesis.

–Prognosis is favorable especially in children.

II-Atypical or Secondary type:

1-Pneumococcal type: It is more common in children < 1 year with 25% mortality despite treatment. It is caused by the neuraminidase of the pneumococci → cleavage of sialic acid from red cell membrane → exposure of Thomsen-Friedenreich cryptic antigen (T Ag) which has a naturally occurring IgM antibody → hemolysis, thrombocytopenia and microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. 2-Congenital: It is usually represented during childhood with high mortality and frequent recurrence. Autosomal recessive mutation of complement regulating proteins as factor H, factor I, membrane co-factor protein (MCP) or factor B → ↑ C3 activation → membrane deposition → renal injury → severe renal impairment 3-Immune (atypical):It is caused by auto-antibodies against factor H. 4-Drug-induced type (atypical):Chemotherapeutic drugs → renal endothelial injury. 112

Original page 113

•Pathogenesis: Pathogenesis of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before”.

•Clinical picture: Clinical picture of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before” with history of bloody diarrhea 7-10 days before the symptoms appear.

•Laboratory investigations: Investigations of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before”.

–Diarrheal type: Shigatoxin identification: Culture of stool or rectal swab is positive for E.coli O157 H7 followed by molecular identification of shiga toxin.

–Pneumococcal type: Positive blood culture and PCR and positive expression of T antigen on red blood corpuscles.

–Congenital and immune type: Serum complement C3 and H factor is low and detection of mutation in the affected gene.

•Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis of thrombotic microangiopathy “see before”.

Treatment

–Antibiotics.

–Supportive care with dialysis.

–Plasma exchange for the immune type.

–Blood transfusion is limited in the pneumococcal type to decrease the exposure of anti-T IgM antibodies.

–Congenital cases may require kidney or liver-kidney transplantation.

•Prevention: Pneumococcal type can be prevented by the pneumococcal vaccine. 113

Original page 114

Post-operatoive thrombocytopenia

•Definition: It is a fall in the platelet count below 150X10/L that occurs after surgeries. 9

Pathogenesis

–Consumption: Immediately after surgery in blood. It returns toward normal in 2–3 days.

–Infection: Viral and bacterial infections.

–Drug induced thrombocytopenia: With antibiotics or heparin.

–Post-transfusion thrombocytopenia.

–DIC: due to severe infection, severe bleeding or severe injury to the endothelium.

–TTP: As a result of severe injury to the endothelium of the blood vessels.

Diagnosis of the cause of postoperative thrombocytopenia

–History: Medications, transfusion, infection, or liver disease.

–Physical examination: Infection, splenomegaly, liver disease and thrombosis.

–Laboratory diagnosis:

○Complete blood picture: Thrombocytopenia with different degrees.

○Blood film: Shistocytes in DIC and TTP.

○Indirect bilirubin: High in DIC, TTP and liver affection.

○Haptoglobin: Low in DIC and TTP.

○PT and APTT: Prolonged in DIC.

○Fibrinogen level: Low in DIC.

Treatment

–Stop of the causative drug.

–Platelet transfusions for platelets 114

Original page 115

Acquired platelet dysfunction

1-Drugs as heparin and antiplatelet drugs. 2-Foods: Onion extracts, garlic and Omega-3 fatty acids nwhich replaces thephospholipid arachidonate by phospholipids rich in eicosapentaenoic acid which is a poor substrate for thromboxane A2 synthesis →↓ thromboxane A2 synthesis. 3-Alcohol: Acquired storage pool defect and ↓ thromboxane A2 production due to inhibition of prostaglandin endoperoxide synthesis. 4-Anti-platelet antibodies as ITP and systemic autoimmune diseases as SLE:

–↓ Interaction between platelets glycoproteins and plasma or matrix proteins → ↓ platelet adhesion, aggregation and clot retraction.

–Acquired deficiency of dense granules.

–↓ Signal transduction that regulates the release of granule contents → ↓ secretion. 5-Uremia:

–Proteolytic degradation of GPIb.

–Acquired VWD.

–Conformational changes in GPIIb/IIIa and ↓ its interactions with fibrinogen.

–Significant ↓ of platelet fibrinogen.

–Structural changes of thrombospondin-1.

–↑ Plasma prostacyclin → receptor-mediated increase of platelet intracellular cAMP.

–↑ Nitric oxide synthase activity →↑ NO →↑ Intracellular cGMP l→↓ inositol triphosphate synthesis and Calcium mobilization →↓ platelet activation.

–Significant ↓ in the platelet production of thromboxane A2.

–Signal transduction defect. 6-Severe liver disease. 7-Cardiopulmonary bypass:

–Drugs: heparin and protamine.

–Platelet activation and fragmentation in non-endothelial bypass.

–Loss of receptors and acquired storage pool defect. 115

Original page 116

8-Major surgeries. 9-DIC. 10-Hyperfibrinolysis. 11-MPN:

–Hyperviscosity.

–Acquired VWD.

–Cyclooxygenase deficiency.

–Thromboxane synthetase deficiency.

–Decreased sensitivity to thromboxane A2.

–Acquired storage pool defect.

–Decreased receptors expression. 12-Myelodysplastic syndrome: Dysmegakaryopoiesis → Dysfunctional glycoproteins → acquired Bernard Souleir disease, aggregation defect like the Glanzman’s thrombathenia and defective platelet spreading. 13-Leukemia:

–Abnormal platelet aggregation due to deficient GPIIb/IIIa.

–Cyclooxygenase deficiency.

–Thromboxane synthetase deficiency.

–Acquired storage pool defect. 14-Vitamin C deficiency → ↓ synthesis of hydroxyproline and therefore of collagen. 15-Paraproteinemia:

–Increased viscosity.

–Paraproteins binding to platelet Fc receptors →↓ interactions between platelet receptors and matrix/plasma proteins → defective adhesion and aggregation.

–Decreased VWF with its coating with paraproteins → acquired VWD.

–Decreased GPIIIa expression and specific binding of paraproteins to it → aggregation defect like the Glanzman’s thrombathenia.

–Renal affection. 116

Original page 117

Diagnosis of platelet dysfunction

1-Detailed history: Bleeding, family history, medical history and drug history. 2-Laboratory investigations:

–Complete blood count: Thrombocytopenia and may be other abnormalities explaining the present disorder.

–Exclusion of Von Willebrand disease.

–Exclusion of coagulation factor deficiencies.

–Exclusion of fibrinolysis disorders.

–Screening tests:

○Bleeding time: Prolonged but it is not sensitive.

○Platelet function analyzer (PFA-100): Closure time is prolonged.

–Platelet function tests: Impaired.

Treatment of platelet dysfunction

–Desmopressin.

–Tranexamic acid.

–Recombinant activated Factor VII.

–Platelet transfusion in severe cases. 117

Coagulation Factors Disorders

Original page 119

Inherited Coagulation Factors Disorders

•Definition: They include chromosomally transmitted quantitative and qualitative abnormalities of the coagulation factors.

Hemophilia:

•Definition: It is an inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of Factor VIII (Hemophilia A), Factor IX (Hemophilia B) or Factor XI (Hemophilia C).

Types of hemophilia

–Hemophilia A: Factor VIII deficiency.

–Hemophilia B: Factor IX deficiency.

–Hemophilia C: Factor XI deficiency.

–Para-hemophilia: Factor V deficiency.

–Acquired hemophilia: Factor VIII inhibitor.

–Autosomal hemophilia: Type 2N Von Willebrand disease. Hemophilia A: It is an X-linked inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of Factor VIII.

•Etiology: Recessive mutations in the Factor VIII gene on the X chromosome: Inversion (50%) of cases, frame-shift mutation, substitution or Tip-flip mutation resulting in Factor VIII deficiency through either instability, abnormal interaction with phospholipids, Factor IX or VWF or inability of activation by Thombin.

Pathogenesis

–↓ Factor VIII → ↓ tenase complex and thrombin burst → friable clot → mechanical dislodgment or easy digestion by fibrinolysis.

–↓ Thrombin → ↓ Thrombin Activitavitable Fibrinolysis Inhibitor (TAFI) → ↑ fibrinolysis.

Clinical picture

–X-linked: Affect mostly males. Carrier females don’t bleed except in some cases.

–Variable bleeding episodes:

➢Factor activity > 20%: asymptomatic. 119

Original page 120

➢Factor activity of 10-20%: Minor symptoms as post-traumatic bleeding.

➢Factor activity of 2-10%: Post-traumatic and occasional spontaneous bleeding.

➢Factor activity < 2%: Severe spontaneous hemarthrosis and joint deformity.

–Presentations according to age: 1-Neonates: Birth trauma as cephalhematoma and bleeding after circumcision. 2-Infants: Large bruises after picking up and minor knocks. 3-Walking infants: Joint bleeding.

Complications

–Joint and muscle bleeding: Entrapment neuropathy.

–Hemarthrosis: Joint deformity and debilitating arthritis.

–Intracranial hemorrhage: ↑ Intracranial pressure which may be fatal.

–Complications of the treatment are:

➢Transfusion transmitted infection as hepatitis C and B and HIV.

➢Development of acquired factor inhibitors.

Laboratory diagnosis

1-Diagnosis of a case:

–Normal platelet count and function.

–Normal bleeding time, prothrombin time and thrombin time.

–Prolongation of clotting time and activated partial thromboplastin time.

–Mixing tests show correction after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma.

–Immunological and Functional factor assays: ↓.

–VWF Ag and Ristocetin co-factor assay are normal.

–DNA analysis detects the causative defect. thth

–Prenatal diagnosis: Genetic testing of a chorionic villous sample 11-14 wks.

2-Diagnosis of female carriers:

–Factor VIII level: Variable in female carriers according to the degree of inactivation of the normal X chromosome.

–DNA probe or RFLP: Detect the genetic defect. 120

Original page 121

Differential diagnosis of Factor VIII deficiency

–Some hemophilic carriers.

–Acquired hemophilia due to an acquired inhibitor to Factor VIII.

–Combined deficiency of Factor V and Factor VIII.

–VWD.

–DIC.

Cause of high Factor VIII levels

–Black races.

–A and B blood groups.

–Acute inflammation.

–Exercise.

–Pregnancy or Contraception.

–Liver cirrhosis.

Hemophilic females

–A daughter of a carrier mother and a hemophilic father.

–Turner syndrome which has one X chromosome.

–Autosomal hemophilia.

–Acquired hemophilia.

–High degree of lionization: Inactivation of a high percentage of the normal X chromosome.

Treatment

–Factor VIII: Concentrate, plasma-derived purified or recombinant.

–Cryoprecipitate.

–Fresh frozen plasma.

–Desmopressin.

–Gene therapy. Hemophilia B: Less common and milder but females may bleed.

–Molecular defect: Deletion (40-50%) or mutation (30%) 121

Original page 122

Hemophilia C: Bleeding is severe after surgeries in areas with high fibrinolytic activities because Factor XIa activates the thrombin activitable fibrinolysis inhibitor (TAFI). Bleeding may be immediate or delayed.

122

Original page 123

Inherited Fibrinogen Defects: Chromosomally transmitted quantitative and qualitative abnormalities of the fibrinogen.

Classification

1-Quantitative defects: Hypofibrinogenemia and Afibrinogenemia. 2-Qualitative defects (Dysfibrinogenemi). 3-Combined quantitative and qualitative defects (Hypodysfibrinogenemia). Inherited Dysfibrinogenemia:Autosomal dominant variants of fibrinogen with abnormal structure and function and normal level as Fibrinogen Baltimore, Okalhoma, Detrui and Paris I.

•Pathogenesis: The abnormal structure causes inability of fibrinogen to either:

–Polymerization (group I): Bleeding tendency.

–Conversion to fibrin by the action of thrombin (group II): Bleeding tendency.

–Stabilization by Factor XIIIa: Bleeding tendency.

–Degradation by fibrinolysis: Thrombosis.

–Thrombin binding: ↓ Thrombin incorporation into the clot → ↑ Thrombin → Thrombosis.

–Impaired fibrin mediated plasminogen activation: Thrombosis.

Clinical picture

–Very mild bleeding or thrombotic manifestations.

–Delayed wound healing.

–Hereditary renal amyloidosis: Extracellular deposition of abnormal fibrinogen in the kidney.

Laboratory findings

–Platelet aggregation and clot retraction may be impaired or e enhanced.

–Normal immunological assays for fibrinogen and defective functional assays. Inherited Afibrinogenemia: Autosomal recessive near-complete absence of the fibrinogen.

–Fibrinogen by immunological methods < 20 mg/dl (N: 200 – 400) and ↓ functional assays.

–↓ Platelet aggregation, ESR and blood viscosity. Inherited Hypofibrinogenemia: Inherited quantitative decrease of the fibrinogen level: Fibrinogen by immunological methods: 20 - 100 mg/dl. {N: 200 – 400}. 123

Original page 124

Inherited combined Factor V and VIII Deficiency: Autosomal recessive deficiency of both Factor V and FactorVIII caused by mutation of either:

–Lectin-Mannose binding protein-1 (LMAN-I) gene which is responsible for the intracellular transport of these factors.

–Multiple Coagulation Factors Deficiency-2 (MCFD2) gene which acts as a cofactor for the LMAN-I. Inherited Factor VII Deficiency: Isolated prolongation of PT. It may be normal because not all reagents are sensitive to Factor VII deficiency. Inherited Factor XII Deficiency: Factor XII deficiency causes no bleeding because:

•It is not found in plasma but in tissues and is released at stress.

•It doesn’t only ↑ coagulation but also ↑ fibrinolysis and ↓ platelet aggregation.

•Factor XI can be activated by platelets through Collagen Induced Coagulant Activity (CICA) and Contact Product Coagulant Activity (CPCA). Inherited Prekallekrin Deficiency: It causes no bleeding but causes:

–↑ APTT which is shortened by increasing the contact time.

–Kinin deficiency.

–Fibrinolysis defects.

–Defective chemotaxis. Inherited HMWK Deficiency: ↑ APTTwhich is not shortened by ↑ contact time. 124

Original page 125

Inherited Factor XIII Deficiency:

Clinical picture

–Severe bleeding several hours after injury.

–Poor wound healing.

–Repeated abortion.

Laboratory diagnosis of Factor XIII deficiency

1-Clot solubility test :

•Principle: Fibrin clot formed in the presence of Factor XIII is stable for in 5 mol/1 urea while in the absence of Factor XIII, clot resolves rapidly. The test is more sensitive when the sample is clotted by thrombin.

•Method: Patient plasma is mixed with an equal volume of 10 NIH (National 0 Institute of Health) unit thrombin solution and is incubated for 20 minutes at 37C and the urea solution is added with a careful dislodgement of the clot and then is 0 left undisturbed for 24 hours at 37C with inspection at regular intervals.

•Interpretation: The test is abnormal if the clot is resolved after 24 hours.

2-Immunological assays.

Inherited Deficiency of Vitamin K Dependent Factors: Autosomal a hereditary dysfunction of γ-glutamile carboxylase enzyme → poorly carboxylated Factor II, Factor VII, Factor IX, Factor X, Protein C, Protein S and Protein Z.

•Clinical picture: Severe bleeding and may be associated with skeletal abnormalities.

•Treatment:

–Oral or parenteral massive dose of vitamin K1.

–Fresh frozen plasma.

–Prothrombin complex concentrate. 125

Original page 126

Acquired Coagulation Factors Disorders

•Definition: Acquired quantitative and qualitative abnormalities of the coagulation factors.

Etiology

1-Vitamin K deficiency. 2-Liver disease. 3-Renal disease. 4-Cardiopulmonary bypass. 5-Circulating anticoagulants. 6-Drugs. 7-Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. 8-Primary Hyperfibrinolysis. 9-Massive transfusion. 10-Massive trauma. 11-Malignancy. 12-Pregnancy. 13-Paraproteinemia. 14-Amyloidosis. 126

Original page 127

Coagulopathy of Vitamin K Deficiency

Definition: It is a bleeding disorder resulting from vitamin K deficiency which is necessary for the function of the coagulation factors; FII, FVI, FIX and FX.

Etiology

1-Dietary deficiency. 2-Malabsorption. 3-Liver disease. 4-Obstructive jaundice. 5-Hemorrhagic disease of newborn. 6-Antibiotics: Kill the intestinal bacteria which synthesize vitamin K. 7-Anticonvulsants. 8-Oral anticoagulants: Inhibit the hepatic vitamin K reductase → preventing the regeneration of active vitamin K for carboxylation of the terminal glutamic acid of vitamin K dependent factors (Factor II, Factor VII, Factor IX, Factor X, Protein C, Protein S and Protein Z) → ↑ PIVKA → negative feedback by saturation of hepatic surface receptors → ↓ sytnthesis of these factors. Protein C has the shortest half-life leading to a hypercoagulable state in the beginning of use of oral anticoagulants.

Diagnostic criteria

I-Prothrombin time is more than 4 fold of normal.

II-One of the following:

1-Normal platelets, normal fibrinogen and absent FDPs. 2-Normalization of coagulation tests after parenteral vitamin K. 3-Positive PIVKA.

Treatment

–Vitamin K: Oral or intravenous.

–Fresh frozen plasma.

–Prothrombin complex concentrate. 127

Original page 128

Differential Diagnosis

Hemorrhagic Disease of Newborns: A bleeding disorder during the first few days of life caused by deficiency in vitamin K.

Etiology

–Poor passage of vitamin K across the placenta and absence of vitamin K in breast milk.

–Prematurity of liver enzymes.

–Maternal intake of anticoagulants or anticonvulsants.

–Delayed gut colonization due to delayed breast feeding, vomiting severe diarrhea or antibiotics including maternal antibiotics.

Classification

128

Original page 129

•Diagnostic criteria: Diagnostic criteria of itamin K deficiency “see before”.

•Treatment: Treatment of vitamn K deficiency “see before”.

Differential Diagnosis

129

Original page 130

Disseminated Intravascular Coagulopathy

•Definition: It is an acquired thrombo-hemorrhagic disorder characterized by diffuse intravascular microthrombosis with loss of localization and secondary hemostatic defect through consumption of coagulation factors and platelets.

Etiology and Pathogenesis

1-Initiation: Excess activation of coagulation → excess thrombin → multiple fibrin clots in the circulation → trapping of platelets → larger clots → microvascular and macrovascular thrombosis. 1-Inflammation:

–Thrombin interacts with endothelial cell PAR receptors → ↑ cytokine → ↑ negatively charged phospholipids on inflammatory cells → vicious circle.

–The acute phase response ↑ fibrinogen and other proteins.

–IL1 and TNF ↑ TF expression on monocytes and macrophages.

–IL6 ↑ platelet count and activity.

–Thrombin converts C5 to C5a while the mannan binding pathway of complement converts prothrombin to thrombin.

–C4b binding protein binds and ↓ PS → ↓ anti-inflammatory function of PC.

–Reactive oxygen species↑ nuclear factor-k B → ↑ transcription of cytokines.

2-Endothelial cell activation leading to:

–↓ Thrombomodulin and EPCR due to down regulation and depletion.

–↑ PAI.

–↑ Ultra-large VWF.

–Collagen exposure. 3-Sepsis:Especially gram negative septicemia:

–Endotoxin: ↑ TF expression on macrophages and monocytes and activates Factor XII.

–Increased circulating microparticles from platelets and granulocytes.

–Inflammation.

–Endothelial cell activation. 4-Malignancy: See cancer induced coagulopathy “see after”. 130

Original page 131

5-Massive Trauma:See trauma induced coagulopathy “see after”. 6-Obstetric complications: See obstetric coagulopathy “see after”. 7-Large aortic aneurysm/ Vascultis. 8-Giant hemangioma:Consumption of PLT and coagulation factors. 9-Transfusion reactionsas n ABO incompatibility hemolytic reaction. 10-Severe allergic or toxic reactionsas in snake or viper venom. 11-Liver disease (chronic DIC): See coagulopathy of liver disease “see after”. II-Fibrinolysis:Excess circulating thrombin → activation of plasminogen → fibrinolysis:

–Excessive plasmin degrades fibrinogen and other coagulation factors → consumption of coagulation factors and platelets.

–FDPs have powerful anticoagulant properties through:

○Interfering with normal fibrin polymerization

○Binding to the platelet surface GPIb/IIIa inhibiting platelet aggregation.

–Excess plasmin activates the complement and kinin systems leading to shock, hypotension, and increased vascular permeability.

III-Dissemination: due to:

–Persistence of the initiating etiology.

–Decreased levels of anticoagulants:

○Consumption.

○Neutrophil elastase degrades the anti-thrombin III.

○Decreased expression of thrombomodulin and EPCR due to endothelial cell damage and downregulation.

–Fibrinolytic shutdown:

○Increased TAFI due to the high level of thrombin.

○Increased PAI due to endothelial cell activation.

IV-Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA).

V-Bleedingdue to consumption of platelets and coagulation factors. VI-Organ damage: The lodging of clots in the microcirculation, in the large vessels, and in the organs is what → Ischemia, impaired organ perfusion, and end-organ damage. 131

Original page 132

Clinical picture

–Compensated DIC: ↑FDPs and normal platelets and coagulation factors with no hemorrhage or thrombosis.

–Clinical DIC: ↑FDPs and ↓ platelets and coagulation factors with hemorrhage and thrombosis:

○Bleeding: the most prominent manifestation ranging from oozing at puncture sites to major gastrointestinal tract or intracranial hemorrhage.

○Organ failure: due to microvascular thrombosis: Renal, Liver, Nervous system, Pulmonary and Adrenal Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

○Shock: may be caused by DIC itself or by its underlying cause.

○Mortality: may be caused by DIC itself or by its underlying cause.

Laboratory diagnosis

–CBC: Normocytic normochromic anemia and thrombocytopenia with a rapidly declining platelet count.

–Blood film: prominent red cell fragmentation. This is a non-specific and a non-sensitive.

–↑ APTT, PT and TT with the biphasic waveform of APTT independent on prolongation.

–Coagulation factors assay:

○Early ↓ Factor V and Factor VIII because fibrinolysis attacks them earlier.

○↓ Fibrinogen: It may be increase in the early stages of 50% of cases because it is an acute phase reactant.

–Positive markers of fibrinolysis: FDPs, ↑ D-dimer, X fragments and Y fragments, ↑ Bβ15- 42 fragment and ↑ Plasmin-antiplasmin complex.

–Positive markers of thrombin generation: Thrombin – Antithrombin complex.

–Positive markers of fibrin generation: Fibrinopeptide A and B.

–Positive markers of activated platelets: PF4, β2 thromboglobulin and P-selectin.

–↓ Anticoagulants as the antithrombin III and Protein C. 132

Original page 133

Differential diagnosis

➢Diagnostic algorithms:

➢Does the patient have any underlying cause of DIC?

–Yes: Proceed.

–No: don’t use this algorithm.

➢Calculate the score:

–If it is > 5: Overt DIC.

–If it is <5: Daily repetition of the score.

133

Original page 134

Treatment

1-Treatment of the cause.

2-Management of bleeding:

➢Fresh frozen plasma

➢Platelet concentrate in dangerous bleeding only.

➢Cryoprecipetate.

➢Prothrombin complex concentrate.

➢Fibrinolytic inhibitors are contraindicated because fibrinolysis lyses thrombi in organs.

3-Management of thrombosis:

➢Heparin use is of controversy.

➢Recombinant activated Protein C.

➢Antithrombin III concentrate: in DIC with liver disease.

➢Anti-platelet as aspirin low dose.

➢Recombinant Anti-IL I. 134

Original page 135

Primary Hyperfibrinolysis

•Definition: Primary increase in fibrinolytic activity in the absence of coagulation when excess plasmin is produced due to release of large amount of tissue plasminogen activator into blood resulting in bleeding.

Etiology

1-Severe liver disease: the most common. 2-Thrombolytic therapy. 3-Malignancy e.g.: Cancer prostate and endometrial carcinoma. 4-Prostatectomy. 5-Idiopathic.

Pathogenesis of coagulopathy

–Fibrinogen and fibrin degradation products which act through:

○Inhibition of thrombin (anti-thrombin IV).

○Inhibition of fibrin polymerization.

○Coverage of platelet receptors and inhibition of platelet aggregation.

–Consumption of coagulation factors. 135

Original page 136

Laboratory findings

•Treatment: antifibrinolytic drugs as epsilon amino caproic acid (EACA) which may be contraindicated in DIC. 136

Original page 137

Coagulation Factors Inhibitors

•Definition: These are antibodies that neutralize specific clotting factors in vivo or inhibit phospholipid-bound proteins in vitro (antiphospholipid antibodies).

Types of circulating inhibitors

1-Antibodies to factor complex which inhibit the interaction between coagulation factor complexes on the phospholipid surface. 2-Antibodies to specific factors:

–Auto-antibodies: Antibodies produced by the self-immune cells and are directed against self-coagulation factors.

–Allo-antibodies: Antibodies produced by the immune cells of one person and are directed against coagulation factors of another person. 137

Original page 138

Specific Coagulation Factors Inhibitors

•Definition: These are antibodies that neutralize specific clotting factors in vivo.

Etiology

–Idiopathic in 50% of cases.

–Acquired mutation.

–Autoimmune diseases as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis.

–Alloimmune antibodies may develop after factor supplementation.

–Paraproteinemia.

–Skin diseases as pemphigoid.

–Pregnancy.

–Drug induced as with penicillin and sulpha.

–Repeated blood transfusion.

–Factor V inhibitor: xposure to topical thrombin which contains traces of Factor V.

–Prothrombin inhibitor: Lupus anticoagulants through cross reactivity.

•Clinical picture: Spontaneous severe life-threatening subcutaneous bleeding, mucosal bleeding, gastrointestinal bleeding and genitourinary bleeding. Hemarthosis is uncommon.

•Laboratory findings: Diagnosis must be preceded by exclusion of lupus anticoagulants.

Vitamin K antagonists

•Mechanism of action: It inhibitsvitamin K epoxide reductase and vitamin K reductase that is required for regeneration of the active form of vitamin K → ↓ active form of vitamin K → ↓ gamma carboxylation of the terminal glutamic acid residue of the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors; Factor II, Factor VII, Factor IX and Factor X and vitamin K dependent anticoagulants; protein C, protein S and Protein Z → PIVKA which can’t bind to the phospholipid surfaces to form the coagulation complexes.

–The deficiency of each of the vitamin K dependent factor begins according to the half- life of each factor which are 5 hrs for FVII, 48 hrs for FX, 24 hrs for FIX and 72 hrs for FII leading to an imbalanced deficiency of vitamin K dependent factors for several days and prolonged PT with no appropriate anticoagulant effect.

–The half-life of protein C is 8 hrs → rapid deficiency of it with the use of vitamin K antagonists with a theoretic thrombosis. LMW heparin must be started with the start of vitamin K antagonists for 5 days or more (48 hrs after reaching the target INR).

–Diarrhea.

–Malnutrition.

–Liver disease decreases synthesis of coagulation factors and impairs their metabolism decreasing drug sensitivity.

–CYP2C9 or VKORC1 polymorphism decreases the catabolism of the drug potentiating its action.

–Hereditary resistance to the drug with a decreased affinity of the coumarin receptor decreases its action and requires very large doses. 173
